title: DriveWorld3D Evidence Constrained 3D World Modeling and Generative Simulation for Real-World Autonomous Driving
summary: Three dimensional modeling for autonomous driving must continuously estimate road geometry, obstacle occupancy, traffic participant behavior, and observational uncertainty under limited computational resources. Existing reconstruction methods can synthesize realistic novel views, but visual fidelity does not sufficiently characterize the geometric reliability required for driving. Generative world models can expand scenarios and predict future observations, yet may introduce content unsupported by measurements. We propose DriveWorld3D, a framework combining temporal video learning, measurement constraints from multiple sensors, and offline generative simulation. Its online component maintains a unified world state comprising road surfaces, volumetric occupancy, dynamic entities, and road relations, while separately representing physical occupancy, observability, and evidence provenance. Action conditioned future prediction and risk sensitive planning connect this representation to driving decisions. Its offline component reconstructs recorded scenes using neural radiance fields or 3D Gaussian Splatting, then expands long tail conditions using generative models while restricting the use of generated content as geometric ground truth. We specify data partitioning, sensor ablations, fault injection, paired closed loop testing, and real to simulation consistency assessment. The central hypothesis is that explicit evidence management can reduce dangerous false free space predictions and occlusion risk within a matched computational budget while retaining acceptable driving efficiency. All performance claims remain subject to experimental validation. Keywords: autonomous driving; 3D occupancy; sensor fusion; uncertainty; generative world models; NeRF; 3D Gaussian Splatting; closed loop simulation

title: Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents
summary: Robot learning has advanced by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. The resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement. We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration: enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales. In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by +37.4% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions. As exploration scales, we observe emergent capabilities including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot collaboration. We open-source RAX as a generalist robot-agent platform in which new robot embodiments are integrated through their APIs alone, without teleoperated data collection or policy training.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what we have discovered. Building in our discoveries only makes it harder to see how the discovering process can be done. --- Richard S. Sutton, The Bitter Lesson~ Robot learning has made substantial progress by scaling demonstration data and model capacity with imitation learning, aiming to replicate the training recipe that transformed language modeling~ kaplan2020scaling . Vision-language-action (VLA) models and World-Action models (WAMs) fine-tune pretrained VLMs and video generation models, respectively, using large teleoperation corpora~ brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0 . However, deploying a new robot or task still requires a dedicated teleoperation corpus of its own~ o2024open,team2024octo,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_,bjorck2025gr00t,liu2026g0,wang2026openwam,yuan2026fast,kim2026cosmos,bi2026motus . Furthermore, the knowledge of such policy models is inherently bounded by the demonstrations they imitate. Consider a mobile robot tasked with loading a car in an unfamiliar house: while opening doors, grasping bags, and placing objects may each be familiar skills, the robot must adapt to novel scenes, visual appearances, and task compositions while discovering new approaches. This adaptation and discovery process is absent during imitation learning on static teleoperation data. Consequently, these policies struggle to generalize and self-improve, even when provided with environment interactions and test-time compute. This limitation motivates a central question: can robots self-improve and learn to discover new skills through autonomous online experience and active exploration? Humans learn physical skills by attempting a task, observing the outcome, diagnosing failures, and practicing until their behavior becomes reliable. LLM agents exhibit a similar pattern in software domains: they explore unfamiliar systems by executing programs, inspecting outputs, and revising their work~ yang2024swe . Instead of training policies exclusively on teleoperated demonstration data, we let agents program robots directly~ 1456949 without hand-designed action primitives. The agent explores online to discover decisions that drive task success, then automates these decision-making principles into modular robot programs that integrate perception, planning, and control. It continuously debugs and tests these programs through online execution. These programs encode the agent's underlying principles for how to generate successful actions based on environment perception, rather than merely mimicking the actions themselves, thereby enabling more robust generalization. Furthermore, the agent can compose, modify, and update these programs when confronting increasingly complex scenes and tasks, continually improving through online experience. We introduce (Robot Agent eXploration), a cognitive architecture for robot agents. Its core organizing principle is scaling exploration: robot agents should improve by gathering their own online experience and optimizing their programs. In , a general-purpose coding agent receives a natural-language instruction, at most a few goal images or visual demonstrations, and a budget of exploration episodes. It interacts directly through the robot's perception and control interfaces without requiring human teleoperation or value function guidance. The underlying language model parameters remain fixed and no policies are trained; instead, learning updates a persistent workspace of programs, notes, and verified skills. The agent converts successful interactions into autonomous code programs and stores reusable knowledge for subsequent episodes and tasks. As exploration scales, we observe several emergent system capabilities: the agent constructs task-relevant 3D perception models, plans actions via pose search in 3D joint space, generates fully automated programs with closed-loop visual and force feedback, and adapts its programs when encountering novel task conditions. Furthermore, we observe agentic behaviors on real robots, including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and active human-robot interaction. For example, the robot executes end-effector contact probing for precise localization when depth measurements are inaccurate. In mobile manipulation experiments, following an initial collision with a cabinet, the agent automatically instantiates a safety check to verify workspace clearance before every base rotation. To test code robustness, the agent actively requests the human operator to vary object layouts, systematically testing the spatial generalization of the autonomous program. In , we equip the agent with rich multimodal sensing by exposing metric depth and force signals through the robot interface. A unified architecture supports tabletop bimanual arms, dexterous hands, mobile household robots, and humanoids through interfaces to each robot's sensors, controllers, and kinematic models ( ). Unlike standard VLAs or WAMs operating on RGB images alone, the agent autonomously leverages these rich sensing signals to construct 3D point clouds and fit object models directly from perception. It then searches for actions to manipulate these 3D models while accounting for their unique shapes and affordances. Force feedback further enables the agent to resolve spatial uncertainty through contact and enable close-loop control on force signals in insertion tasks. Such multimodal world modeling have been largely absent from generalist policy models, yet naturally align with human cognitive processes. To enable high-frequency closed-loop control, the agent compiles its decision-making process into executable Python programs that generate actions directly from sensor signals. Unlike prior approaches that rely on human-designed action primitives or policies trained on demonstrations lu2026aspire, xiao2026enpire , our approach directly generates robot control programs that encapsulate the full perception-planning-control loop, whereas standard policies discard the underlying decision-making process essential for generalization. In practice, we observe the agent writing programs that automatically segment and identify objects in 3D using point-cloud fitting and hue-based identification, then plan actions grounded in this 3D world model, with retry loops and exception handling naturally incorporated into the code. Because actions are planned directly on perceived 3D objects rather than learned through imitation, this approach generalizes to far more diverse object layouts and domain variations than standard VLAs or WAMs. For semantically rich perception in open-world environments, the agent can program direct API calls to LLMs (such as Gemini) within the code to assist with object identification, while incorporating checkpoints and exception handling to step in and verify progress. Over the course of exploration, both action inference latency and token counts decrease as an increasing fraction of decisions becomes automated through code. As experience scales with exploration, maintains an intra-task memory file system across episodes to record failure lessons and successful strategies, allowing the agent to continually refine its programs. Across multiple tasks and sessions, we maintain a repository of modular programs as verified skills for various tasks and manipulation primitives. Each skill includes the executable code for a specific task, accompanied by execution logs from successful runs, clear preconditions, and verification checkpoints, allowing skills to be composed and reused for complex downstream tasks. In real-world mobile manipulation experiments in household settings, the agent practices individual tasks, each in its own exploration session, such as picking and placing boxes or tucking in office chairs, and commits them as verified skills. When subsequently evaluated on a composite, long-horizon task involving more than six sequential object manipulations, the agent achieves substantial automation and efficiency gains by reusing these stored skills. We envision agents practicing skills in a distributed, parallel fashion to build a rich repository of diverse capabilities, thereby enabling continual lifelong learning. Using , we conduct the first large-scale, multi-embodiment, systematic study of scaling exploration for robot agents, spanning fine-grained precision and long-horizon tasks across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, RoboDojo, DexJoCo, BEHAVIOR-1K, and HumanoidArena in simulation and on two real robots. We evaluate the resulting policies on unseen scenes, separating exploration from evaluation. Performance grows steadily with exploration, and on fine-grained and long-horizon tasks on which state-of-the-art methods rarely succeed, achieves high success rates, surpassing the strongest prior models by +37.4 on average over five benchmarks ( , ). Without any expert action trajectories, sets a new state of the art on RoboDojo (+53.4), BEHAVIOR-1K (+38.3), DexJoCo (+31.4), and LIBERO-Pro (+21.2). On HumanoidArena, it sets a new state of the art (+7.9) with three teleoperated demonstrations per task, where every baseline uses 100. On real Franka and Rainbow RB-Y1 robots, masters five complex tabletop manipulation tasks and a long-horizon mobile manipulation task with zero demonstrations, and verified skills accumulated across sessions let later sessions build on earlier ones. We summarize our contributions below: We introduce and establish scaling online exploration as a foundational principle for agentic robotics. In , the agent operates directly through perception and robot control interfaces without policy training, compiling successful decision sequences into executable code programs that run autonomous execution loops. Using , we conduct the first systematic, multi-embodiment study of scaling online exploration across simulation and real robot environments. acquires diverse manipulation capabilities solely through autonomous exploration, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by points on average across five simulation benchmarks, while solving high-precision, deformable, articulated, and long-horizon manipulation tasks on real robots without human demonstrations. We demonstrate rapid adaptation and continual learning on real robots, showing that generated programs can be selectively updated in response to environmental and task shifts while retaining verified skills in a persistent repository for composition and reuse in complex tasks. We release the full architecture of , together with its agent instructions, skills, benchmark integrations, and evaluation protocols, as a generalist robot-agent platform, on which a new robot can be brought up through an interface alone, without data collection or policy training. SayCan grounds language-model plans in learned affordances~ ahn2022can , Inner Monologue folds environment feedback into iterative replanning~ huang2022inner , and Code as Policies, ProgPrompt, and VoxPoser synthesize executable programs, situated task plans, or 3D value maps directly from instructions~ liang2023code,singh2022progprompt,huang2023voxposer . title: KFS$^4$LAM: Adaptive KeyFrame Selection with Structure-Aware Mapping for Endoscopic Gaussian Splatting SLAM
summary: Gaussian-splatting Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) augments conventional SLAM with a dense, renderable 3D scene representation, enabling high-quality reconstruction and novel-view synthesis. However, its localization, reconstruction, and rendering performance depends strongly on which observations are retained for mapping. Existing systems commonly rely on fixed temporal intervals or simple pose- and overlap-based criteria for keyframe selection. In colonoscopy, non-uniform camera motion, repetitive anatomy, specularities, and visual artifacts can make these criteria unreliable, leading to either redundant keyframes or missed informative viewpoints. We present KFS$^4$LAM (KeyFrame Selection with Structure-aware mapping for endoscopic Gaussian Splatting SLAM), which couples motion-guided adaptive keyframe selection with structurally supervised mapping and restricted temporal deformation. Accumulated motion guides adaptive keyframe selection, with complementary cues suppressing redundant or unreliable candidates. Density-aware mapping with anatomical contour supervision (colon folds) emphasizes structurally informative regions, while restricted temporal deformation accommodates local tissue dynamics without unconstrained geometric drift. We evaluate KFS$^4$LAM against Gaussian-SLAM baselines on C3VD and C3VD-v2, together with cross-backbone and component ablations. KFS$^4$LAM achieves strong overall performance across trajectory, rendering, and depth metrics, with pronounced gains on more challenging C3VD-v2 dataset. In the matched comparison with SplaTAM on C3VD-v2, it reduces rotational relative pose error by 20.3% and depth RMSE by 38.4%, while improving PSNR by 0.78 dB. Cross-backbone experiments further show that the framework is not tied to a single underlying SLAM architecture. Code and visualization results are available at https://xinweiju.github.io/KFSLAM/.

Accumulated motion guides adaptive keyframe selection, with complementary cues suppressing redundant or unreliable candidates. Density-aware mapping with anatomical contour supervision (colon folds) emphasizes structurally informative regions, while restricted temporal deformation accommodates local tissue dynamics without unconstrained geometric drift. We evaluate KFS LAM against multiple Gaussian-SLAM baselines on C3VD and C3VD-v2, together with cross-backbone and component ablations. KFS LAM achieves strong overall performance across trajectory, rendering, and depth metrics, with particularly pronounced gains on the more challenging C3VD-v2 dataset. Cross-backbone experiments further show that the framework is not tied to a single underlying SLAM architecture. Code and visualization results are available at Project Page . Introduction Accurate camera tracking and dense reconstruction from endoscopic video can support spatial navigation, anatomy/lesion localization, and procedure documentation ~ dunnbeltran2024nflba,muhlethaler2022coverage . However, endoscopic scenes differ markedly from the rigid, well-textured environments assumed by conventional SLAM, exhibiting deformable tissue, a restricted field of view, specular reflections, non-uniform illumination, and repetitive or texture-poor anatomy~ dunnbeltran2024nflba . Camera motion is also highly non-uniform, causing the information contributed by consecutive frames to vary substantially. Slow or near-stationary motion produces long runs of near-redundant observations, whereas rapid translation, rotation, or viewpoint change can reveal substantial new scene content within only a few frames. Consequently, treating observations uniformly can devote mapping effort to redundant views while overlooking more informative ones, making observation selection an important factor in both camera tracking and reconstruction quality. Compared with earlier implicit neural representations~ nice_slam , 3D Gaussian Splatting represents the scene using explicit, efficiently renderable anisotropic Gaussians, enabling localized map updates and high-quality rendering, as demonstrated in GaussianSLAM~ yugay2023gaussianslam , MonoGS~ matsuki2024gaussiansplatting , and SplaTAM~ keetha2024splatam . Recent endoscopic methods have improved robustness to deformable tissue and weak texture through endoscopy-specific tracking in EndoGSLAM~ wang2024endogslam , deformation-aware representations~ zhu2024endogs,liu2024endogaussian , and stronger geometric regularization such as surface-conforming constraints, normal supervision, and pose-aware keyframe strategies~ huang2025endo2dtam,bonilla2024gaussianpancakes . However, these advances have primarily focused on tracking, scene representation, and map optimization, with comparatively less attention to adaptive observation selection and the explicit use of persistent anatomical structure during mapping. Keyframe selection in conventional SLAM is commonly based on geometric and visibility cues such as displacement, parallax, and covisibility~ campos2021orbslam3,lsdslam . Related criteria are also widely used for view selection in structure-from-motion and multi-view reconstruction~ schonberger2016sfmrevisited,schoenberger2016mvs , while more recent approaches have explored richer geometric and photogrammetric criteria~ pks and learned, data-driven selection policies~ rl_keyframe_vo . In endoscopy, however, assessing viewpoint novelty from visual and correspondence cues remains challenging due to specular reflections, illumination variation, tissue deformation, weak texture, and repetitive anatomy~ ozyoruk2021endoslam,azagra2022endomapper,bobrow2023c3vd . These effects can produce substantial appearance or correspondence changes without necessarily indicating a geometrically informative new viewpoint~ rota2025endoscopicmatching . Existing endoscopic Gaussian-SLAM systems largely rely on temporally spaced keyframes in EndoGSLAM~ wang2024endogslam or pose/overlap-driven policies in Endo-2DTAM~ huang2025endo2dtam , with limited consideration of observation redundancy and reliability under non-uniform camera motion. Beyond keyframe selection, anatomical structures such as colon folds can complement appearance-based geometric reasoning~ ju2024segcol,ju2026multimodal and provide persistent spatial constraints for endoscopic navigation and reconstruction~ dunnbeltran2026centerline . Incorporating such structure into Gaussian mapping therefore offers a complementary source of supervision to RGB appearance. Building on these observations, we introduce KFS LAM, a structure-aware Gaussian-SLAM framework that couples motion-guided adaptive keyframe selection with structurally supervised mapping and restricted temporal deformation. Rather than allowing appearance change to directly trigger keyframe insertion, accumulated camera motion proposes candidate viewpoints, while complementary image- and feature-level cues suppress unreliable or redundant candidates. The resulting non-uniform keyframe density is accommodated by adapting the mapping budget to the number of retained keyframes. The selected observations are further integrated with anatomical fold supervision and restricted temporal deformation, using persistent fold structure to regularize Gaussian mapping while accommodating local non-rigid tissue motion. Taken together, KFS LAM provides an adaptive mapping strategy that balances viewpoint informativeness, observation efficiency, and structural consistency in deformable endoscopic scenes. Our evaluation shows consistent improvements in localization and map quality without relying on a higher keyframe density, with the benefits becoming more pronounced on the more challenging C3VD-v2 sequences. Component and cross-backbone ablations further indicate that these gains arise from the proposed design rather than from increased mapping effort or a particular Gaussian-SLAM backbone. The main contributions of this work are: A motion-guided adaptive keyframe policy that combines accumulated-motion-based candidate proposal with redundancy-aware visual suppression. A structure-aware mapping design that combines density-aware mapping with anatomical fold-boundary supervision and fold-conditioned restricted temporal deformation, providing complementary image-space structural supervision and a soft spatial prior for non-rigid Gaussian motion, enabling non-uniform observation allocation under varying camera motion. A comprehensive evaluation on C3VD and C3VD-v2, including component and matched cross-backbone ablations that isolate the effects of adaptive keyframe selection, structural supervision, and restricted temporal deformation, and demonstrate consistent improvements across different Gaussian-SLAM backbones. title: When Plans Change, Remember: Replanning-Guided Visual Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Long-horizon, multi-stage Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies often require visual information that is no longer present in the current observation. Retaining the complete observation history is computationally expensive and highly redundant, motivating selective visual memory. We introduce RePlanMem-VLA (Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA), which turns a policy's own plan revisions into an online memory-write signal. Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions. RePlanMem-VLA treats unusually large disagreement between these temporally aligned predictions as evidence of a task-relevant event. We first compare 35 disagreement measures across single-task autoregressive decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformers trained from scratch, then validate the selected signals on pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and $π_{0.5}$ policies over MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks. The resulting detectors achieve ROC-AUC of 0.981-0.997. We then use the selected signals in RePlanMem-VLA to trigger updates to a bounded visual memory, with a robot-masked write filter suppressing redundant frames. In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision point in 100% of episodes. Real-robot replay data further show that event selection and redundancy suppression extend beyond simulation. These results establish plan revision as a policy-internal signal for controlling what a VLA remembers. Website: https://vika787.github.io/RePlanMem/.

When consecutive replans disagree on their overlapping actions, the important observation is stored in memory and remains available after the cue is no longer visible. fig:visual-abstract Introduction sec:introduction Long-horizon manipulation often requires Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies to use visual information that has left the current observation, including object properties~ chen2026rmbench,shi2026memoryvla , earlier environment states~ chen2026rmbench,shi2026memoryvla , and task progress~ buamanee2026bihil,feng2026procvlm . Retaining the full history preserves these cues but increases context length and computation while adding visual redundancy~ jang2025contextvla,qiu2026efficientlonghorizonvla,wang2026nativemem . We therefore seek a small set of informative observations. We call these observations keyframes: they preserve cues needed later~ shi2026memoryvla,lei2026robomemarena or mark task-phase transitions~ buamanee2026bihil,yi2026criticlooptrisystemvla . Prior work selects them with vision-language models~ lei2026robomemarena , waypoint heuristics~ shi2023waypoint , learned retrieval~ sridhar2025memer , progress estimates~ liu2026palm , or event detectors~ zeng2026kemo . We investigate whether the policy's own plan revisions can provide an online signal for selecting these observations. Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions, while the new plan incorporates the latest observation (Fig.~ fig:visual-abstract ). Comparing these temporally aligned predictions reveals how the policy revises its intended behavior after receiving new visual information. Our central hypothesis is that task-relevant observations induce unusually large revisions in predictions for the same future actions. This motivates using plan disagreement as a policy-internal signal to identify candidate keyframes for visual memory. We introduce RePlanMem-VLA (Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA), which derives its selection signal from revisions between overlapping action predictions already produced during normal replanning. Selected keyframes become part of the policy's visual context, keeping past observations available for subsequent action prediction, while a robot-masked write filter suppresses redundant frames, reducing repeated overwrites. At deployment, the trigger requires neither keyframe annotations nor privileged simulator state. Our experiments are conducted on MIKASA-Robo-VLA~ cherepanov2026mikasarobovlabenchmarkingmemoryvla , an extension of MIKASA-Robo~ cherepanov2026memory for evaluating memory-intensive manipulation with VLA policies. We first screen 35 disagreement metrics using autoregressive decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformers~ lipman2023flow trained from scratch. We then evaluate detectors based on the selected signals with pretrained OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025oft and ~ pi05 policies, obtaining ROC-AUC of 0.981--0.997. In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision point in \(100 \) of episodes, while robot-masked filtering reduces redundant overwrites. Real-robot replay data further support its event-selection and redundancy-suppression behavior beyond simulation (Fig.~ fig:real-robot-setup ). Our main contributions are as follows: We introduce RePlanMem-VLA, which identifies keyframes from policy-internal revisions of predictions for the same future actions across consecutive replanning steps (Section~ sec:plan-revision-signal ). We identify disagreement measures that best align with keyframe events through systematic analysis across decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformer policies, and verify their transfer to pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and policies (Sections~ sec:rq1-metric-screening and~ sec:rq2-vla-keyframe-detection ). We develop a bounded visual-memory mechanism where plan disagreement determines when to write and redundancy-aware filtering, including robot-masked clustering, determines what to retain, substantially reducing redundant updates while preserving task-relevant observations (Sections~ sec:method and~ sec:rq3 ). title: PASS-VLN: Passability-Aware Local-Command Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Reliable vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires not only understanding instructions but also determining whether and how a robot can physically execute them. However, existing VLN benchmarks typically assume executable instructions and focus on long-horizon tasks. This leaves body-dependent local execution, including passability and collision-free execution, largely unexamined. Evaluating these factors within long-horizon tasks would entangle local physical execution with task planning and long-term spatial memory, making navigation failures difficult to attribute. We therefore focus on grounding local navigation commands in executable motion under environmental and robot body constraints. We present PASS-VLN, a passability-aware local-command VLN benchmark and model. The benchmark holds the scene, instruction, start pose, and reference route fixed while varying robot body width, requiring target completion when the instructed passage is feasible and stopping before blockage otherwise. Our model encodes body width through obstacle inflation in a depth-derived local bird's-eye view, fuses geometry with visual and linguistic context, and predicts discrete latent action codes for continuous closed-loop execution. Experiments show that PASS-VLN improves collision-free success by approximately 12 percentage points over a strong VLN model fine-tuned on our benchmark, while adapting reach-versus-stop behavior to body constraints and generalizing to unseen body widths. When integrated with a high-level planner, PASS-VLN achieves higher success with fewer local commands, while real-world deployment further demonstrates its effectiveness as a low-level executor. The benchmark and model will be released.

Introduction Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow natural-language instructions and navigate to a target in visual environments. R2R established the standard indoor VLN setting~ anderson2018vision , followed by benchmarks for more complex multilingual instructions~ ku2020room , continuous control~ krantz2020beyond , remote object grounding~ qi2020reverie , persistent navigation~ krantz2023iterative , and physics-aware unified evaluation~ lin2025vlnverse . Most existing VLN benchmarks provide a complete route instruction per episode and assume that the instructed motion is physically executable. Directly incorporating body-dependent physical execution, including passability and collision-free execution, would couple local execution with planning, progress tracking, spatial memory, and route-level reasoning, making navigation failures difficult to attribute. Many recent VLN methods emphasize stronger reasoning, memory, and planning~ rajvanshi2024saynav,zhou2024navgpt,zheng2024navillm,qiao2025opennav,lin2026evolvenav, xin2026agentvln,wang2026reflectvln,guo2026awarevln , whose gains do not necessarily translate into improved local physical execution. Conventional navigation methods based on local mapping and motion planning account for traversability and collision constraints, but typically take geometric goals or reference paths as input without a natural-language interface for interpreting spatially grounded commands~ hart1968formal,fox1997dynamic,rosmann2013efficient . These considerations motivate focusing on local physical execution as a capability that complements high-level reasoning and memory. A human or a high-level agent, including one based on a VLM, can issue local commands, while a low-level executor grounds each command in current observations and converts it into physical motion. The local command serves as their semantic interface, specifying an immediate local objective and the spatial cues needed to interpret it. For example, ``move forward and stop between the sofa and the table'' specifies landmarks, spatial relations, and a stopping condition while leaving broader task planning to the command issuer. Such a local executor must reason about not only where to go, but also whether and how the motion can be physically executed. Most existing VLN research emphasizes semantic spatial reasoning, such as left/right relations, object ordering, relative positions, and path structure~ wang2023gridmm,huo2023geovln,dai2024optimal,zhang2025mapnav, zhu2025mtu3d,zeng2025janusvln , without explicitly considering physical spatial feasibility under body constraints. In practice, a correctly grounded passage may still be too narrow for the robot, and traversable passages may require body-dependent clearance and alignment. A local executor should therefore consider the instructed motion and its physical feasibility under the current embodiment. To address these requirements, we introduce PASS-VLN, a PASSability-aware local-command VLN framework comprising a controlled benchmark and a body-width-conditioned model for planar physical execution. The benchmark holds the scene, instruction, start pose, and reference route fixed while varying robot body width. For paired configurations where passage feasibility changes under the same command, the narrower robot is expected to reach the target, whereas the wider robot is expected to stop before the blockage, directly testing whether execution adapts to the interaction between instructed motion, environmental geometry, and robot embodiment. The benchmark covers commands based on local observations and commonsense spatial knowledge for visible-target navigation or bounded exploration, as well as commands requiring broader scene or route knowledge. To connect language understanding with body-dependent geometry and motion execution, PASS-VLN projects depth into a local bird’s-eye view (BEV) and incorporates body width through obstacle inflation, making the geometric representation reflect robot-specific clearance. Fusing this representation with language, current vision, and visual history allows the policy to interpret the instructed motion in relation to its physical feasibility. To translate this understanding into continuous execution, the model predicts discrete latent action codes learned from short trajectory windows, which are decoded into planar relative motions for closed-loop control. The main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce a controlled VLN benchmark that isolates local execution from long-horizon navigation and explicitly evaluates body-width-dependent physical feasibility. Its paired counterfactual design tests whether an agent changes its reach-versus-stop behavior under different body constraints while preserving the command’s semantic intent. We develop a body-width-conditioned VLN model for local physical execution. Body-conditioned geometry allows the same policy to adapt passability decisions and motion execution across seen and unseen widths, while discrete latent actions preserve VLM-style token prediction and enable continuous closed-loop motion. Experiments demonstrate generalization to unseen body widths and improved collision-free success over the evaluated binary passability-gating baseline. In a shared reference-route-assisted hierarchical pipeline, PASS-VLN achieves higher collision-free navigation success with fewer local commands, while real-world deployment further validates its practical utility. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-and-Language Navigation Benchmarks subsec:vln_benchmarks R2R introduced instruction following in photorealistic indoor environments~ anderson2018vision , while RxR increased linguistic diversity through multilingual instructions and dense spatiotemporal grounding~ ku2020room . VLN-CE moved navigation from discrete graphs to continuous environments with low-level actions~ krantz2020beyond . REVERIE combined navigation with remote object grounding~ qi2020reverie , and Touchdown studied navigation and spatial reasoning in outdoor street-view environments~ chen2019touchdown . AerialVLN extended the task to UAV navigation~ liu2023aerialvln , and VLNVerse introduced a scalable physics-aware framework covering multiple VLN tasks and embodied agents~ lin2025vlnverse . PASS-VLN complements these benchmarks by isolating local-command spatial grounding and explicitly evaluating whether the local motion specified by an instruction remains physically executable under different body widths, including unseen widths. title: Ego2Contact: Predicting Touch from Egocentric Human Video for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
summary: Contact locations and interaction forces are critical for contact-rich robot manipulation but are often ambiguous from vision alone. Measuring them on robots requires specialized tactile hardware and platform-specific data collection, which keeps robot tactile data scarce. Human egocentric video is far easier to scale but lacks touch. Recent predictors trained on egocentric recordings paired with tactile-glove measurements can predict this missing signal from video alone. These predictors, however, remain confined to human hands, which differ from robot hands in appearance and tactile layout. We present Ego2Contact, which learns a visual-tactile prior from human interactions and transfers it to robot hands. Its predictor fuses temporal scene context with hand-local visual features to infer bimanual tactile fields from the RGB video. Anatomical region correspondences align varying robot tactile layouts with the predictor's canonical grid, turning robot measurements into fine-tuning targets and predictions into policy inputs. Ego2Contact outperforms prior tactile predictors on human data, including unseen objects, and on robot data after adaptation. The adapted predictor provides tactile inputs for both simulated reinforcement learning and real-robot policy post-training. In simulation, policies using predicted touch outperform non-tactile baselines and recover part of the benefit of ground-truth tactile sensing. These results show that human-learned tactile priors can supply touch when direct tactile sensing is limited.

Introduction Reliable contact-rich robot manipulation depends on understanding where physical contact occurs and how interaction forces evolve. Dexterous behaviors, from regulating grip force against slip to detecting contact onset under occlusion, rely on contact information that is often ambiguous from visual observations alone~ johansson2009tactile,calandra2018feeling . Tactile sensors provide direct measurements of these interactions, yet collecting large-scale visual-tactile data on robots remains challenging. Tactile skins and optical sensors require specialized hardware that is difficult to integrate and tightly coupled to specific end-effector geometries~ dahiya2010tactile,gelsight . Consequently, tactile recordings are costly to collect and difficult to reuse across platforms, leaving tactile measurements largely absent from large-scale cross-embodiment datasets~ openx . Human egocentric video, by contrast, is far easier to collect at scale~ epickitchens,ego4d,egodex but lacks touch. Recent datasets recorded with sensing gloves pair egocentric RGB video with dense full-hand pressure measurements~ opentouch,touchanything,egotactile . Training a predictor on such data makes it possible to recover this missing signal directly from visual observations, without a tactile sensor at inference time. However, existing visual-tactile predictors are developed and evaluated exclusively within the human domain~ pressurevision,touchanything,egotactile , and they do not show that inferred touch can drive robot policies. In contrast, robot-centric approaches that imagine or predict tactile signals learn entirely within a single robot's native sensor space and do not draw on human interaction data~ tacimag,vitacworld . Methods that do transfer human tactile priors to robots entangle tactile estimation with a specific policy architecture or action space~ vtdexmanip,htac . What remains missing is a unified mechanism that extracts a generalizable visual-tactile prior from human interactions and delivers it to heterogeneous robots as explicit tactile observations that their policies can consume. Establishing this human-to-robot bridge involves two fundamental challenges. The first is to resolve the visual ambiguity during contact inference. Since the interacting surfaces are routinely occluded by the hand, a static image or an estimated 3D hand pose does not uniquely determine the underlying pressure distribution. Identical hand configurations can exert vastly different forces depending on the task phase. Therefore, reliable inference demands integrating the temporal dynamics of the scene with fine-grained local hand appearance. The second challenge is to overcome the morphological and sensory discrepancy between human and robot hands. Robot hands differ visibly from gloved human hands, which shifts the visual input away from the human training distribution. A predictor trained on human gloves also produces pressure on a human-centric layout, whereas the downstream robots may rely on sparse rigid-link force readings in simulation or high-density taxel arrays in the real world. Without a structured interface, predictions in human space cannot be supervised by robot measurements or consumed by robot control policies. We introduce Ego2Contact, a framework that learns a visual-tactile prior from human egocentric video and transfers it to robot hands, where it provides tactile observations for robot learning (Figure~ fig:teaser ). Ego2Contact formulates tactile estimation as conditional flow-matching generation over a canonical 2D hand-grid representation~ touchanything . To address the visual ambiguity, our diffusion transformer is conditioned on a cross-attentive fusion of temporally aggregated scene tokens and hand-local visual features. The canonical grid organizes tactile signals into explicit anatomical regions, so it naturally serves as a cross-embodiment interface. By establishing region-level correspondences between this grid and a target robot's physical sensing zones, we map distinct robot tactile recordings into the canonical space for fine-tuning and decode the generated grid predictions into policy-compatible tactile inputs. Fine-tuning on paired robot video also adapts the predictor to the robot's visual appearance. Because the predictor outputs explicit tactile observations, it remains decoupled from the downstream policy and serves both reinforcement learning and vision-language-action (VLA) post-training. We validate Ego2Contact across the perception-to-action loop. In tactile prediction, our method outperforms regression and pose-conditioned baselines across seen and unseen objects on human data, as well as after adaptation to collected robot data. More importantly, the adapted predictor functions as a virtual tactile sensor that provides link-level contact features for reinforcement learning in simulation, and it generates dense tactile images from demonstration videos to post-train a VLA policy on a real dexterous hand. In simulation, policies consuming predicted touch improve over non-tactile baselines and recover part of the benefit of ground-truth tactile sensing. In summary, this work has the following contributions. We propose Ego2Contact, a conditional flow-matching visual-tactile generator that fuses temporal scene context with hand-local visual features to synthesize accurate bimanual pressure fields from egocentric video. We establish an anatomical adaptation interface that aligns human tactile priors with different robot sensor topologies, turning robot measurements into fine-tuning targets and canonical predictions into policy-compatible inputs. We evaluate Ego2Contact from human tactile prediction to simulated reinforcement learning and real-robot VLA post-training, showing in simulation that vision-inferred touch improves the success rate of contact-rich manipulation over non-tactile baselines and recovers part of the benefit of real tactile sensing. Related Work Vision-Based Contact and Pressure Estimation Predicting physical interaction from images has progressed from localizing contact to estimating continuous pressure. Early datasets capture where contact occurs on object or hand surfaces~ brahmbhatt2019contactdb,taheri2020grab , and dense predictors estimate the binary hand-surface contact~ haco . A parallel line regresses hand pressure from RGB, from planar touchpads~ pressurevision,pressurevisionpp to egocentric observations with pose and mesh-space pressure~ egopressure,egopressdiff . Recent work scales this to full-hand tactile fields by pairing egocentric video with wearable-glove measurements~ touchanything,egotactile,egotac,opentouch,htbench , and estimates contact and 3D force jointly from monocular input~ egophi,hope,rlhnd . Among these, TouchAnything introduces the EgoTouch dataset and a bimanual predictor whose canonical layout we adopt~ touchanything . These methods show that dense touch is visually predictable, but they operate and are evaluated within the human domain. Tactile Sensing and Imagination for Robot Manipulation Tactile feedback improves contact-rich control when vision is ambiguous. Policies combine visual and tactile observations to select regrasping actions~ calandra2018feeling and to react to force feedback during execution~ reactivediffusionpolicy . Multimodal visual-tactile representations support contact-rich tasks~ lee2019makingsense , and tactile sensing has enabled dexterous skills such as in-hand object rotation from vision and touch~ guzey2023dexterity,qi2023rotateit . Since tactile hardware is not always available at deployment, a line of work predicts tactile signals within the robot's own domain. TacImag learns a vision-to-touch model from paired robot demonstrations and supplies imagined tactile to sensor-free policies~ tacimag , while ViTacWorld learns an action-conditioned visuo-tactile world model from robot trajectories for rollout generation and policy learning~ vitacworld . These approaches rely on robot-collected tactile data and do not leverage the scale of human interaction data. Transferring Human Priors to Robot Tactile Learning Beyond extracting visual representations~ nair2022r3m or motion trajectories~ qin2022dexmv,shaw2022videodex,wang2024dexcap from egocentric datasets~ damen2018epic,grauman2022ego4d,hoque2025egodex , recent efforts have begun transferring human tactile priors to robots. VTDexManip~ vtdexmanip pretrains visual-tactile representations from human demonstrations to accelerate dexterous reinforcement learning, whereas H-Tac~ htac learns a joint tactile-action latent space that transfers to robots via post-training. In particular, both paradigms entangle tactile estimation with a specific policy architecture or action space. Ego2Contact instead decouples perception from control, learning a dense pressure predictor from human video and bridging robot sensor layouts via anatomical correspondences. The predictions are evaluated as observations for both simulated and real-world policy training. title: MambaAct: Efficient Mamba Action Experts for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains a major bottleneck for real-time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow-matching VLAs such as $π_{0.5}$, where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising. We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder of $π_{0.5}$, while replacing its transformer-based action expert with a compact Mamba-based action expert. Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous-action sequence. To preserve visual-language conditioning without repeated token-level cross-attention, MambaAct uses a lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision-language model (VLM) prefix tokens into a compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block. MambaAct uses a $10\times$ smaller action expert and reduces flow-matching denoising latency by $64.8\%$ on LIBERO and $58.8\%$ in real-world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by $1.08$ percentage points across three independent fine-tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks. Our code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct.

Introduction Recent flow-matching VLAs such as ~ black2024pi_0 and ~ black2025pi_0 achieve strong manipulation performance, but their iterative action-generation process introduces substantial inference cost. At every policy query, the visual-language prefix can be computed once, whereas the action expert must be evaluated repeatedly across multiple flow-matching denoising steps. As a result, action generation can become the dominant source of latency even when the visual-language backbone itself is relatively compact. Recent efforts to improve VLA efficiency have largely reduced this cost by decreasing the number of sampling steps, compressing or pruning pretrained networks, reducing visual-token processing, or redesigning the policy around smaller architectures. While effective, these approaches primarily accelerate inference by reducing how often existing components are evaluated or by simplifying the visual-language pathway and overall model. In contrast, the architecture of the repeatedly evaluated action expert itself remains comparatively underexplored as an efficiency axis. This motivates us to ask whether flow-matching inference can instead be accelerated by replacing the action-generation module while preserving the pretrained visual-language representations and standard flow-matching formulation. We address this question with MambaAct, a compact Mamba~ lahotimamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language encoder and replaces its large Transformer-based action expert with a lightweight Mamba sequence mixer. Mamba is attractive in this setting because its selective state-space formulation provides a compact inductive bias for modeling ordered, strongly correlated action sequences. As we show empirically, this design enables aggressive action-expert compression while preserving policy performance. To efficiently condition the newly initialized expert on the pretrained VLM, we introduce a Context Compressor and gated FiLM~ perez2018film interface that transform the visual-language prefix into a compact representation reused throughout flow-matching denoising. The resulting expert contains only M parameters, compared with M for the original action expert. Our main contributions are: We introduce MambaAct, establishing action-expert replacement as a complementary efficiency axis for flow-matching VLAs. MambaAct replaces the repeatedly evaluated Transformer action expert with a compact Mamba expert while retaining the pretrained visual-language backbone and standard flow-matching formulation, without additional pretraining or distillation. We show that Mamba enables aggressive action-expert compression: MambaAct uses over fewer action-expert parameters than while improving mean LIBERO~ liu2023libero success by percentage points across three fine-tuning seeds. title: Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting
summary: N-dimensional splatting extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with view direction and time to model view-dependent and dynamic effects. Each primitive is lifted into a joint distribution over position and conditioning variables, then conditionally sliced at each rendering query. N-DGS and UBS share this step across Gaussian and Beta kernels: recovering the conditional mean, opacity, and covariance requires per-primitive matrix inversions and regression products in every forward pass. We introduce direct conditional parameterization, replacing this covariance-derived readout with explicit per-effect parameters: a Cholesky precision factor for opacity and a factorized query-to-position regression operator with learnable per-dimension coupling. Unrestricted conditional coordinates recover a valid joint covariance; our factorization adds spatial-scale and coupling priors. Applied to both kernels, the parameterization yields dGS (Gaussian) and dBS (Beta). Across five static and dynamic benchmarks, they match or exceed their covariance-derived counterparts on quality, with gains up to +1.26 dB in the main MCMC evaluation. Production slicing is 6.9-7.7 times faster than on-the-fly covariance-derived conditioning; complete-render profiling gives 1.25-1.91 times speedups on four trained scenes. Introduction sec:introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs achieves photorealistic novel-view synthesis at real-time speeds through explicit 3D Gaussian primitives. Static primitives, however, struggle with specular reflections, temporal dynamics, and view-dependent geometry. Recent work extends 3DGS along two orthogonal axes. The first is kernel shape: alternatives to the Gaussian kernel include Beta kernels~ liu2025deformable,liu2025universal , generalized exponentials~ hamdi2024gesgeneralizedexponentialsplatting , and Student-t distributions~ zhu20253dstudentsplattingscooping . The second is dimensionality: N-dimensional Gaussians (N-DG)~ diolatzis2024n , refined as 6DGS~ gao20246dgs and 7DGS~ gao20257dgs (collectively N-DGS), lift each primitive into a joint distribution over 3D position and conditioning variables (view direction with , view+time with ). At render time, the -dimensional primitive is conditionally sliced at the current query (a view direction or timestamp) using the conditional Gaussian formulas: the mean shifts, the opacity is modulated by a kernel evaluated at the query, and the spatial covariance receives a correction term. Universal Beta Splatting (UBS)~ liu2025universal combines the two axes by replacing the Gaussian opacity decay with an anisotropic Beta kernel while inheriting the same conditional-slicing structure. N-DGS and UBS together represent the leading N-dimensional splatting formulations across Gaussian and Beta kernels. title: VLA-Fabric: Learning Interaction for Composable Multi-Arm VLA Agents
comment: 17 pages, including references and appendices. Project website: https://nebulis-lab.com/VLA-Fabric/
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are rapidly expanding what individual robots can accomplish, yet many real-world manipulation settings require multiple arms to operate as a coordinated system. Existing approaches organize multi-arm coordination in different ways, including centralized joint policies, high-level task or role assignment, and locally executed policies that react to teammates. However, how complete action-producing VLAs should explicitly interact with one another during action generation remains largely unexplored. We introduce VLA-Fabric, which organizes one complete VLA per arm while preserving local perception and action ownership, and enables coordination through learned interaction across policy boundaries. We first systematically study where such interaction should occur, how peer information should be aggregated, and how the interaction should be learned, revealing complementary coordination functions spanning shared context, peer-specific latent information, and action-stage interaction. We then re-instantiate these functions in a structurally different VLA architecture, showing that the coordination principle is not tied to a particular tensor layout or backbone implementation. Finally, we compose teams of three and four arms and evaluate them in simulation and physical experiments. On all four physical tasks, Full interaction improves success over independently trained local policies by 16--40 percentage points. Together, these results suggest that explicit interaction among complete VLA policies offers a scalable path toward networked embodied intelligence.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models are advancing the capabilities of individual robots by connecting visual and language understanding with learned action generation rt2,openvla,pi05 . Many important robotic applications, however, require several manipulators to contribute to a common physical objective. Cooperative manufacturing, multi-part assembly, shared-load handling, and flexible robotic workcells motivate systems in which multiple arms work together cooperative_topp,apexmr,fabrica . As pretrained VLAs become more capable, their progress creates an opportunity beyond improving a single robot: organizing multiple action-producing policies into a collaborative system. The ability of each constituent model to perceive and act does not, by itself, specify how those models should work together. Recent multi-arm VLAs pursue this goal through different organizations. RDT-1B, ET-VLA, TwinVLA, and Dexora place cross-arm dependencies within a joint policy rdt1b,etvla,twinvla,dexora . Other approaches coordinate at different levels: MA-VLA assigns atomic behaviors to individual arms mavla , while CHORUS demonstrates implicit decentralized coordination through locally executed policies that observe and react to teammates without runtime messages chorus . These approaches establish effective collaboration, with coordination inside a joint policy, above the action policy through behavior assignment, or indirectly through observations of teammates. This raises an organizational challenge as the number and roles of manipulators grow. How can a multi-arm system remain modular at the level of individual manipulators while still supporting tightly coupled collaboration? A natural way to obtain such modularity is to organize the system around complete arm-local policies rather than a growing joint policy. We therefore treat each manipulator and its complete VLA as a self-contained execution unit that perceives its local context and produces its own actions. Local information can remain with the policy that uses it, and larger teams can be formed by composing additional execution units. Crucially, local does not mean isolated. Policies participating in the same physical task still need to adapt their actions to one another. The key challenge is to connect these local policies through explicit interaction without giving up their local action ownership. To realize this local-but-connected organization, we introduce VLA-Fabric Project website and code: . , a multi-VLA coordination architecture connecting complete arm-local policies through learned internal representation interaction (Figure~ fig:motivation ). Each VLA retains local perception and action generation while selected peer representations condition its computation through explicit policy interaction. VLA-Fabric thus makes coordination among complete policies an explicit learning and architecture problem instead of absorbing all cross-arm dependencies into a joint policy. First, we establish an effective VLA-Fabric interaction architecture through a broad controlled study. Starting from a decomposable bimanual VLA with pretrained single-arm streams twinvla , we separate its original cross-arm dependencies. We systematically explore a combinatorial design space covering interaction entry points, aggregation operators, and fine-tuning strategies. The study shows that exposing more peer information does not by itself ensure coordination; interaction structure and adaptation determine how effectively local policies use one another's information. This exploration identifies complementary interaction at shared-context, peer-specific intermediate, and action-generation stages. Second, we demonstrate that the same VLA-Fabric interaction paradigm can be re-instantiated in substantially different VLA architectures. We use pi05 as a second realization, whose multimodal processing and action generation differ markedly from the Eagle2 VLM-based SingleVLA used in our initial study. Accordingly, the same coordination functions are realized at architecture-appropriate computational boundaries while preserving complete local policies with explicit policy interaction. The resulting -Fabric system enables multiple complete policies to interact and achieves strong performance across several bimanual tasks. Its stronger results suggest that advances in the constituent VLA may translate into stronger collaborative systems. This observation is consistent with the value of pretrained single-arm capabilities demonstrated by TwinVLA twinvla . Third, we establish the extensibility of VLA-Fabric from bimanual coordination to larger teams of complete VLA policies. Additional manipulators are incorporated by composing additional local policies and extending their interaction. We instantiate three- and four-arm VLA-Fabric teams and evaluate them on simulation tasks with different coordination demands. We further validate the same organization on four physical three- and four-arm tasks, where Full interaction consistently improves over independently trained local policies. title: World Action Critic (WAC) Model: Joint Foresight and Criticism for Policy Learning
summary: World models have shown considerable promise in sequential decision-making by anticipating the consequences of actions and providing predictive foresight for policy learning. However, learning to reason about counterfactual actions remains challenging, since predictive objectives may underemphasize information critical for action evaluation, while unexecuted actions lack observed futures for direct supervision. To address these challenges, we propose the World Action Critic (WAC) Model, which proposes multimodal action candidates and jointly learns candidate-conditioned future prediction and consequence evaluation. In our proposed framework, critic supervision directly shapes intermediate predictive representations during rollout, encouraging them to retain information needed to distinguish action quality. Observed futures supervise prediction for executed actions, while external task-quality targets provide evaluation signals for counterfactual candidates. Through joint optimization, critic signals from these candidates propagate into predictive representations without requiring their observed futures. Our theoretical analysis characterizes critic-guided feature retention and bounds candidate-selection regret. Applied to autonomous driving, WAC achieves 93.4 PDMS on NAVSIM-v1, demonstrating the effectiveness of jointly learning predictive foresight and consequence evaluation.

Introduction sec:introduction World models enable agents to anticipate how their environments evolve under different actions, supporting policy learning in reinforcement learning~ zhan2025Bootstrap,wang2025Offpolicy, ha2018World,guan2021Direct, hafner2025Mastering , robot control~ zhang2026Langevin,zhan2026Harmonized , and autonomous driving~ gao2022Enhance,li2026WorldEngine, wang2024Driving . By predicting future states from current observations and actions, they provide a basis for reasoning about the consequences of alternative actions before execution. This capability also supports efforts to build physics-native intelligence, as explored in models such as Phi-WM~ sunrisingai2026ActEffect . Effective decision making therefore requires predictive representations that preserve the information needed to compare these consequences. Existing approaches integrate world models into policy learning through three main approaches (Figure~ fig:main ). First, predictive representation learning uses future-state prediction as an auxiliary objective to enrich the features consumed by a policy~ min2024DriveWorld,li2024Enhancing,bousmalis2023RoboCat, lan2023SEPT . Second, simulator-based methods use action-conditioned imagined transitions for reward-based policy optimization or model-based planning~ hafner2019Learning,hafner2020Dream,wu2022DayDreamer,li2024Think2Drive,mu2021ModelBased . Predicted states are evaluated using rewards or values~ hansen2024TDMPC2 , while the transition model is primarily learned from predictive objectives. Evaluation therefore provides a downstream criterion for imagined consequences, with limited control over the information retained in the predictive representations themselves. Third, future-conditioned policies and World Action Models (WAMs) bring prediction into action generation, with recent WAMs jointly modeling future states and actions~ du2023UniversalPolicies,zhu2025Unifieda,bi2025Motus,ye2026World,shi2026DriveWAM . Their joint modeling of future states and actions can capture multimodal behavioral alternatives, while the relative task quality of these alternatives remains implicit. Counterfactual action comparison requires an explicit criterion for evaluating the consequences associated with each candidate. Learning world models for counterfactual action evaluation faces two challenges. First, predictive representations can be mismatched with the information needed for decision making. Under limited representation capacity, future prediction can favor dominant environmental variation over subtle details that distinguish action quality, making predictive accuracy an insufficient criterion for decision value~ farahmand2017ValueAware,grimm2020ValueEquivalence,voelcker2023Value,gao2022Enhance . Second, counterfactual actions lack direct future supervision. A recorded transition provides an observed future only for the executed action, while decisions require comparing unexecuted alternatives at the same decision point~ zhang2026Identifiability . External evaluators can supply task-quality targets through simulation and scoring, but these targets leave complete counterfactual future states unspecified. The challenge is to use this evaluation supervision to learn decision-relevant predictions beyond actions with observed futures. To address these challenges, we propose the World Action Critic (WAC) Model, which jointly learns candidate-conditioned future prediction and consequence evaluation. A multimodal policy first proposes diverse action candidates. Each candidate conditions a recurrent transition--critic Transformer that predicts future latent states and accumulates evidence for evaluating the candidate over the full horizon. Asymmetric attention allows the critic to read intermediate predictive features while keeping critic tokens hidden from the transition stream. Critic supervision propagates through these features during joint training, encouraging them to preserve information needed to distinguish action quality. WAC uses complementary supervision to extend this learning to counterfactual actions. Observed futures supervise prediction for executed actions, while an external evaluator supplies candidate-level quality targets for both executed and counterfactual actions. Critic gradients optimize the predictive features along each candidate's rollout, allowing unexecuted alternatives to guide representation learning even when their future observations are unavailable. Building on existing consequence-based trajectory evaluation~ zheng2025World4Drive,li2025EndtoEnd , WAC couples evaluation to intermediate features throughout recurrent prediction under this complementary supervision. The resulting scores provide a common criterion for comparing multimodal candidates based on their predicted consequences. Our theoretical analyses address these two learning challenges: they characterize how critic supervision promotes decision-relevant feature retention in a linear setting and bound candidate-selection regret in terms of critic fitting error, evaluator error, and candidate coverage. We instantiate WAC for autonomous driving and evaluate it on NAVSIM~ dauner2024NAVSIM , achieving 93.4 PDMS on NAVSIM-v1. Controlled ablations examine factual future supervision, recurrent rollout, and critic gradients into predictive features, supporting the complementary roles of future prediction and consequence evaluation. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: We propose WAC, which jointly learns future prediction and consequence evaluation for counterfactual action reasoning, using critic supervision to shape predictive representations for decision making. We develop a recurrent transition--critic architecture with asymmetric attention and complementary supervision, grounding prediction in factual futures while allowing candidate-quality targets to guide learning from counterfactual actions. We provide theoretical analyses of critic-guided predictive feature retention and candidate selection, showing how evaluation supervision promotes action-relevant future representations and establishing a regret bound under evaluator accuracy and candidate coverage assumptions. Latent dynamics support imagination-based policy optimization, trajectory optimization, and visual planning, as exemplified by Dreamer, TD-MPC2, DINO-WM, and BOOM~ hafner2020Dream,hansen2024TDMPC2,zhou2025DINOWM,zhan2025Bootstrap . World models also support exploration augmentation by synthesizing transitions for off-policy learning~ wang2025Offpolicy . This predictive interface extends to physical robot control and autonomous driving, where action-conditioned futures inform behavior learning and planning~ wu2022DayDreamer,wang2024Driving,chen2021Interpretable,guan2022Integrated,guan2026Enhanced . Across these settings, learned dynamics provide a substrate for decision making: policies or planners use predicted states together with rewards, values, or task costs~ li2023Reinforcement . Prediction and evaluation often remain identifiable components, even when trained jointly. This leaves an important design question beyond whether imagination improves control: how should an evaluation objective shape the information retained in the predictive representation itself? World Action Models World Action Models (WAMs) bring future prediction into action generation, extending action-conditioned dynamics toward joint modeling of environment evolution and behavior. UniPi illustrates an early future-to-action interface by translating generated visual plans into actions through inverse dynamics~ du2023UniversalPolicies . More recent models, including WorldVLA, Motus, and DriveWAM, couple future and action modeling through shared generative or temporal representations~ cen2025WorldVLA,bi2025Motus,shi2026DriveWAM . Their common interface uses predictive knowledge to generate or refine behavior, with action preferences potentially encoded in the learned generation distribution. Such preferences do not necessarily provide an explicit task-quality criterion for comparing externally proposed candidates. WAC addresses this complementary problem: evaluating candidate actions supplied by a proposal policy through their predicted consequences, and using evaluation supervision to shape those predictions. World Models for Value Estimation and Candidate Evaluation Prediction and evaluation have been connected at several levels. Value-aware model learning constrains predictive dynamics by downstream decision objectives, recognizing that uniform transition accuracy need not preserve the information most useful for control~ farahmand2017ValueAware,grimm2020ValueEquivalence,voelcker2023Value . At the representation level, World Value Models and World Critic Models connect world modeling with value learning to assess task progress or support policy improvement~ wang2026World,fei2026WCM . title: Unifying Embodied Foundation Models via a Model-to-Policy Formulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as promising approaches to robot learning and control. These models integrate multimodal perception and action generation, but differ in their architectures, output representations, and learning objectives. In this paper, we present a unified, architecture-agnostic probabilistic formulation for embodied foundation models based on stochastic kernels. Our formulation has two key components: (i) we characterize embodied foundation models through conditional output distributions and action-realization kernels, which together induce task-conditioned robot policies; and (ii) we connect pretraining and post-training to policy deployment, accommodating model-specific pretraining objectives and offline or online post-training strategies. We instantiate the formulation for OpenVLA and DreamZero, covering autoregressive action-token prediction and joint video-action generation.
