Introduction Robot learning is moving from task-specific controllers toward embodied AI systems that learn reusable perception-to-action policies across tasks and embodiments~ openxembodiment2024rtx,octomodelteam2024octoopensourcegeneralistrobot . At its current stage, embodied AI largely adapts the broader foundation-model development pipeline to physical interaction~ driess2023palme . This pipeline combines a shared architectural core with three stages: pre-training, post-training, and deployment. The shared architectural core is typically based on the Transformer family, with modality-specific encoders, tokenizers, or output heads added (if needed)~ vaswani2017attention,brown2020language,geminiteam2024gemini15,xu2025qwen25omni,qwenteam2026qwen35omni . First, pre-training learns general representations from large-scale corpora and multimodal collections through model-specific objectives~ brown2020language,geminiteam2024gemini15,qwenteam2026qwen35omni . Specifically for LLMs, the resulting next-token loss follows predictable power-law relations in model size, data, and compute (similarly rigorous scaling laws are less established for other foundation models)~ kaplan2020scaling,hoffmann2022training,yang2025qwen3 . Second, post-training adapts the pretrained model to follow instructions, align with human or verifiable preferences, and improve downstream task performance~ wei2021finetuned,ouyang2022training . Common approaches include supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference optimization (e.g., DPO and KTO)~ ouyang2022training,rafailov2023direct,ethayarajh2024kto . Other routes use reinforcement learning (e.g., RLHF and RLVR, often implemented with PPO or GRPO) or on-policy distillation (OPD)~ ouyang2022training,schulman2017proximal,shao2024deepseekmath,deepseekai2025deepseekr1,agarwal2024onpolicy . Finally, deployment turns the trained model into a reusable inference and reasoning core. The above foundation-model pipeline has shown broad effectiveness across scales and modalities, underpinning recent language and reasoning models (e.g., GPT-5.6 and DeepSeek-V4), multimodal or omnimodal models such as MiniMax M3 and Qwen3.5-Omni, and generative models including FLUX.2~ openai2026gpt56,deepseekai2026deepseekv4,qwenteam2026qwen35omni . The resulting models can also serve as reasoning and perception cores for agents~ hong2026tools . Such agents support tool use, coding, digital-environment interaction, and multi-agent coordination~ yao2023react,schick2023toolformer,yang2024sweagent,wu2024autogen . Can the success of large foundation models be carried into the physical world? The above non-embodied foundation models generally learn a mapping \(f_ : X Y\) from input data to predictions or generated content~ hong2026hyvint . However, for robot learning, embodied foundation models aim to induce a task-conditioned policy that maps the available interaction history and task condition to a probability distribution over robot actions. Fitting a fixed data distribution is insufficient, since a policy must also perform well on the trajectories induced by its own actions~ kaelbling1998planning,ross2011reduction,brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer . Vision-language-action (VLA) models pursue this policy-learning objective by combining visual observations and language instructions to generate robot actions. The Robotics Transformer (RT) series develops this approach from RT-1's discretized action prediction to RT-2's transfer of internet-scale visual-semantic knowledge through autoregressive action-token prediction~ brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer . OpenVLA likewise adapts a pretrained vision-language backbone with an action-token cross-entropy objective, while couples such a backbone to a flow-matching action expert that generates continuous action chunks~ kim2025openvla,black2024pi . Scaling their robot pre-training is constrained by the difficulty of collecting real robot trajectories across diverse tasks, environments, and embodiments~ openxembodiment2024rtx,black2024pi . Video pre-training offers a complementary route to learning motion and scene dynamics from internet-scale data without robot action labels, reducing reliance on embodiment-specific trajectories for acquiring these priors~ assran2025vjepa2selfsupervisedvideo,ye2026world . For control, the value of this pre-training lies in acquiring transferable regularities of physical interaction that support action, rather than visual realism alone~ assran2025vjepa2selfsupervisedvideo . Such priors support control through predictive world models, as in UniPi, which uses inverse dynamics to extract robot actions from generated video plans~ ha2018world,du2023learning . World-action models (WAMs) couple these visual predictions with action generation under language conditioning, as in DreamZero, which adapts a pretrained video diffusion backbone to jointly generate future video and robot actions~ ye2026world . Conditioned on visual history and proprioception, DreamZero uses flow matching within chunks and autoregressive generation across chunks~ ye2026world . Real robot trajectories ground these pretrained representations in embodiment-specific commands and physical transitions, supporting transfer across tasks, environments, and embodiments~ openxembodiment2024rtx,physicalintelligence2025pi05 . Adapting these representations to downstream control can also change the model's outputs, as adds a continuous action expert during post-training after discrete-token pre-training~ physicalintelligence2025pi05 . The resulting outputs must then be converted into executable actions through decoding and action selection or scheduling~ kim2025openvla,black2024pi,ye2026world . These actions change the observations conditioning subsequent predictions, so the deployed policy depends on both the learned output distribution and its realization in closed-loop interaction. A common description must therefore connect these two components with the objectives and data used in pre-training and post-training. Motivated by this connection, we develop an architecture-agnostic probabilistic formulation based on stochastic kernels. title: GRASP: Global-Local Representation Alignment and Spatial-Physical Grounding for Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that directly regress joint-space actions avoid the deployment-time cost of inverse kinematics. However, their training objectives remain misaligned with task success, as joint-space losses ignore the unequal physical consequences of joint errors and visual conditioning lacks explicit focus on hand-object interaction regions. To address these issues, we propose a training-phase prior injection framework for fine-grained bimanual manipulation. First, a physics-grounded flow-matching loss maps the implicit clean-action estimate at every noise level through differentiable forward kinematics (FK) and supervises the resulting Tool Center Point (TCP) pose and inter-arm relative pose, with a bounded noise-level weighting that compensates gradient decay. Second, we introduce a global prediction query group distilled from a frozen DINOv3 teacher through future-frame feature prediction, together with a local interaction query supervised by Grounding DINO at the attention level. Both teachers are removed at inference, and the deployment pipeline is that of a standard joint-space flow policy, adding only the learned query pathway. Simulation and real-robot experiments on long-horizon bimanual tasks show that the two priors are complementary across different deployment settings. The full model excels in in-distribution deployment, while the distilled query branch is preferable under strong visual randomization.

INTRODUCTION Vision-Language-Action models have made significant progress in general robot manipulation, with models such as , OpenVLA, and LingBot-VLA 2.0~ pi05,openvla,lingbotvla2 demonstrating strong manipulation capabilities. Flow-based policies such as generate continuous action sequences through conditional flow matching~ pi0,flowmatching . Such models either predict the End-Effector Pose (EEP) in task space, requiring a real-time Inverse Kinematics (IK) solver that may yield unreachable poses and discontinuous trajectories due to the one-to-many mapping~ kstar , or directly regress the joint configuration, which avoids these issues but may misalign the normalized joint-space loss with physical-space task success. Specifically, standard joint-space regression losses do not explicitly account for the configuration-dependent effects of joint errors on end-effector motion. As a result, similar errors in joint space can lead to substantially different task-space deviations after forward-kinematic propagation. Meanwhile, visual conditioning in VLA models is often learned indirectly from the action objective, which may limit consistent attention to fine-grained hand-object interaction regions. To address these issues, this paper proposes a training-phase prior injection framework for fine-grained bimanual manipulation, along two dimensions: action supervision and visual conditioning. First, rather than applying kinematic regularization to final actions, we supervise the implicit clean-action estimate throughout the flow trajectory: the estimated clean actions at each noise level are mapped through differentiable forward kinematics, and a geometric loss over TCP pose and inter-arm relative pose ties each penalty to its physical consequence. This loss is training-only, and the policy still outputs joint commands directly at inference. Second, we append a global query group and a local interaction query to the input sequence, supervised respectively by predicting the dense future-frame features of a frozen DINOv3 teacher~ dinov3 and by attention-level KL divergence distillation using interaction regions derived from Grounding DINO~ groundingdino , explicitly guiding the model toward hand-object interaction regions. Both teachers are removed at inference. In our evaluation, we conduct both simulation and real-robot experiments, and show that the proposed framework exhibits a number of desirable properties for fine-grained bimanual manipulation: Simulation benchmark: on 50 bimanual tasks from the RoboTwin 2.0~ robotwin2 benchmark, our full model improves the average success rate over the -SFT baseline by 15.1 percentage points in clean settings, while the -Global+Local Query variant improves it by 29.0 percentage points under domain randomization. Real-robot evaluation: on four long-horizon real-world tasks, including make watermelon juice, soda bottle opening, beverage mixing, and clothes folding, our method improves the average success rate by 14.2 percentage points over the baseline. Physically accurate execution: supervision in physical space reduces TCP position error compared with joint-space-only training, confirming that the geometric loss better aligns the optimization objective with physical execution. Interaction-aware perception: the decoupled global--local queries improve manipulation performance under randomized scenes and unseen-language instructions by guiding the policy toward task-relevant interaction regions. In summary, our core idea is to compress task-space physical constraints and visual-teacher spatial priors into the training phase. Experiments in both simulation and real-world settings on long-horizon bimanual tasks show consistent improvements in accuracy and robustness. RELATED WORK Kinematic constraints in the control of dual-arm robots Two common action representations for bimanual manipulation policies are task-space end-effector poses and joint-space configurations. One paradigm predicts the end-effector pose and relies on a cascaded IK solver, but numerical solvers tend to produce discontinuous trajectories near singular configurations. Generative IK methods alleviate this issue through learning~ ikflow , yet they keep kinematic constraints outside the policy. The other paradigm directly regresses the joint configuration, but dimension-wise regression losses ignore the non-uniformity of the physical consequences of errors propagated through the kinematic chain. Ma et al.~ hdp introduced joint supervision over joint-space and task-space representations, while Lv et al.~ kstar incorporated differentiable forward kinematics to regularize pose learning. Different from these formulations, this paper embeds differentiable forward kinematics directly into the training objective of a joint-space policy, unifying TCP pose and inter-arm relative pose into a geometric loss, requiring no inverse-kinematics solver at inference. Visual Query and Distillation Supervision in VLA models Many existing vision-language-action models encode multi-camera observations into dense visual tokens, while the allocation of visual attention is largely learned implicitly from the downstream action objective. Among existing approaches, two directions are particularly relevant. One line introduces learnable query tokens distilled from frozen visual teachers, for example, predicting future scene representations or kinematic evolution from current observations~ vpp,gr2,geopredict . Such supervision remains at the feature level, without explicitly constraining the spatial allocation of attention. The other line injects spatial priors into attention via open-vocabulary detectors~ owlvit , but does not distinguish the responsibilities of global scene semantics from local interaction details. In contrast, this paper introduces two dedicated query sets, a global query group and a local interaction query. The former is supervised by predicting the dense features of future frames produced by a self-supervised vision model~ dinov3 , while the latter is supervised through attention-level distillation from attention distributions derived from detection boxes~ groundingdino . This explicitly guides the model to focus on the hand-object interaction region, with the detector used only during training. title: SimpleVLN: Towards Simple and Frontier Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to ground language in visual observations and make long-horizon decisions. Existing methods often address these demands through task-specific architectures. As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly capable, an important question remains: Have we truly unlocked the potential of native MLLMs for VLN before introducing task-specific architecture? We present SimpleVLN, an architecture-preserving framework developed through studies of navigation formulation, data construction, and optimization. At the formulation level, SimpleVLN combines single-turn decision inputs with fixed-budget global-local memory to efficiently use navigation history without unbounded context growth, while action chunks enable efficient output of multiple primitive actions per model invocation. For data construction, we combine expert demonstrations with policy-dependent DAgger experience and develop a scalable synthesis pipeline that generates large-scale tasks for reinforcement learning. At the optimization level, a progressive IL-DAgger-RL pipeline advances from action imitation to task-level outcome optimization. Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of these three aspects. We instantiate SimpleVLN across multiple MLLM backbones and model sizes, demonstrating its generality. SimpleVLN achieves 76.7% and 80.1% success rates on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE splits, respectively, substantially outperforming existing methods. These results show that the navigation capabilities of native MLLMs can be effectively unlocked without task-specific architectural designs.

title: NestedVLA: Learning to Consolidate and Generate Skills for Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 23 pages, 3 figures. Code: https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026-NestedVLA
summary: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models promise generalist robotic agents, yet consolidating skills learned across heterogeneous tasks and environments remains difficult: training data is fragmented across platforms, joint multi-task training suffers from interference, and model merging tends to introduce parameter conflicts or require architectural changes. We instead advocate a paradigm in which skills are first learned independently and then consolidated post hoc. To this end, we propose NestedVLA, which replaces parameter aggregation with parameter generation: a nested hypernetwork, conditioned on the target task, synthesizes task-adaptive action-expert parameters that compose with a frozen base VLA. Task-specific compressed VLM residuals are retained separately. This formulation enables flexible task-conditioned skill reuse while mitigating interference. Across three RL benchmarks (MetaWorld, ManiSkill, CALVIN), NestedVLA outperforms the strongest model-merging baseline by 41 pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN, pointing toward a storage-efficient route to skill consolidation. Code is available at . Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine visual and language understanding with embodied control~ rt1,rt2,OpenVLA,pi0,pi0.5 . Independently fine-tuning a common backbone produces policies specialized for different robotic benchmarks, but storing one full checkpoint per benchmark duplicates most parameters. Joint multi-task training can avoid this duplication when data from all benchmarks can be pooled. We instead study post-hoc consolidation of policies independently fine-tuned from the same backbone. We seek to consolidate their task-specific parameter updates into a compact representation without pooling the original training data. A natural post-hoc approach is to merge the parameter updates of the fine-tuned policies into a single checkpoint. In VLA models, however, independently learned updates can interfere strongly when combined: in our experiments, simple averaging loses most of the performance of the separate policies. Our weight-space analysis finds weak alignment across major parameter groups, an incompatibility that is particularly consequential in the action expert because it directly governs control (Appendix~ app:conflict_diag ). This observation is consistent with MergeVLA~ fu2025mergevla , which likewise identifies dependencies distributed across action-expert layers as a major obstacle to cross-skill merging. These findings motivate a consolidation strategy that preserves policy-specific parameter structure rather than collapsing all updates into one set of weights. We propose NestedVLA, a framework that shifts the paradigm from parameter aggregation to parameter generation. A hypernetwork embedded in the VLA generates sparse action-expert updates conditioned on the target task, while compressed task-specific VLM residuals are retained separately. The selected updates compose with a shared base to instantiate a task-specific VLA without changing its forward architecture or introducing routing supervision. We evaluate NestedVLA on MetaWorld~ mcleanmeta , ManiSkill~ maniskill , and CALVIN~ calvin using the open-source ~ pi0.5 backbone. NestedVLA outperforms the strongest model-merging baseline by \,pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning within \,pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action models. Recent VLAs cast robotic control as instruction-following on top of pretrained vision-language backbones~ rt1, rt2, OpenVLA, prismatic, pi0, pi0.5 . OpenVLA~ OpenVLA discretizes actions into rare vocabulary tokens for autoregressive prediction; ~ pi0 pairs the VLM with a separate action expert trained via flow matching for continuous action chunks; ~ pi0.5 extends this design to interleave sub-task narration and low-level control. Lighter variants such as VLA-Adapter~ vla-adapter preserve multi-task competence at sub-billion-parameter scales. VLAct uses representation-centric continued pre-training to preserve VLM priors and promote shared action semantics across embodiments~ yang2026vlact . Across this family, multi-task ability is learned from pooled data, requiring co-located datasets and predefined skills. We target the regime where these assumptions break: skills are acquired independently and consolidated after the fact. Parameter-efficient visual adaptation. Prompt- and adapter-based methods offer lightweight alternatives to full fine-tuning of vision backbones. Recent work makes prompts instance-aware, injects structured visual semantics, or searches for layer-specific prompt fusion rules~ xiao2025visual,xiao2026adapting,xiao2026layer . Structured low-rank adaptation further filters task-irrelevant directions and coordinates updates across layers~ xiao2026not , while visual alignment methods address over-reliance on language priors in multimodal models~ xiao2026staying . meng2026ahra propose AHRA, a hierarchical shared--private expert framework that aligns semantic levels while preserving modality-specific evidence. Such methods adapt or organize multimodal representations; NestedVLA instead starts from independently trained VLA policies and consolidates their parameter updates post hoc. Hypernetworks. Using one network to predict the parameters of another dates back to HyperNetworks~ ha2017hypernetworks , with later applications to continual learning~ vonoswald2020continual and multi-task NLP~ mahabadi2021parameter . Recent parameter generators use latent diffusion to synthesize neural-network weights~ wang2024pdiff , scale this process to full models with recurrent generation~ wang2025rpg , map task prompts directly to LoRA weights~ liang2025dnd , or produce instance-conditioned weight updates as functional memory~ wu2026hywu . NestedVLA inherits this task-conditioned generation premise, but targets a sparse top- delta on a frozen billion-scale VLA backbone via patch-based tokenization, and consolidates independently fine-tuned RL policies rather than learning skills from scratch. Reusable task updates. Related work on language models compresses full-model task updates into modular SkillPacks for heterogeneous knowledge fusion and multi-domain specialization~ du2026graftllm,li2026skillweave . HoE instead extracts LoRA-form experts from task vectors and routes them for multi-objective alignment~ li2026hoe . These studies concern text-only language models and retain or select task modules. NestedVLA studies closed-loop VLA policies and generates the action-expert update with an embedded hypernetwork. Model merging. Model merging combines independently trained checkpoints into a single deployable model. Recent surveys organize model fusion across parameter, representation, and behavior levels~ cai2026fusion, zhou2025democratizing,zhou2026model . Static merging produces one fixed delta via weighted averaging~ modelsoup, fishermerging, TA, du2024knowledge , conflict-handling~ ties, dare, wudi, pcb, fang2025see , or low-rank sub-spaces~ tsvm, knots, iso-cts, twin, nps , with adapter counterparts~ pem-composition, do-merging . Dynamic merging retains per-task masks, scalars, residuals, or frequency-domain corrections at inference~ tall-mask, emr, free-merging, mmer, didi2026 . Recent adaptive methods build reusable component-level expert libraries for input-aware recombination~ qiu2026merge or evolve experts with manifold-aware, training-free routing for continual merging~ qiu2026madeit . Across both regimes the operative verb is select: every output value is an interpolation, mask, or projection of values already present in . Complementary studies make expert training merge-aware~ gu2026smat , calibrate or quantize post-merge models~ gu2026featcal,wang2026epmq , and analyze scaling laws or expert-read budgets for weight-space merging~ wang2026modelmergingscaling,wang2026mergepipe . NestedVLA generates the per-skill delta from a single shared hypernetwork instead. Embodied applications of merging remain largely unexplored; ReVLA~ revla mitigates single-skill domain forgetting rather than multi-skill consolidation. NestedVLA sec:method Problem Formulation sec:method_formulation We consider task-specific datasets , each corresponding to a manipulation task in a benchmark-specific setting. Fine-tuning a pretrained VLA backbone on each yields task-specific parameters and the corresponding task vector~ TA which captures all parameter changes induced by task . We treat each as the parametric encoding of a skill, a reusable manipulation capability acquired in isolation. The goal of skill consolidation is to construct a unified model that leverages the entire skill set across diverse downstream scenarios without storing full per-task checkpoints or using expert routing. A common approach is to merge into a single static delta~ TA, ties, modelsoup, fishermerging, wudi . However, parameter aggregation in the VLA setting suffers from severe inter-task conflicts (Sec.~ sec:intro ), as different tasks impose contradictory updates on the same parameters. We instead propose to generate parameters. Write for the VLM and action-expert parameters. In the evaluated v1 system, a generator , conditioned on task identifier , produces the action-expert delta, while a compressed VLM delta is retained for the same task: Both updates compose with the frozen base at inference. This shifts the action-side problem from parameter aggregation to parameter generation, avoiding full per-task checkpoints and a single conflicting merge. Overview sec:method_overview NestedVLA realizes the generator as a hypernetwork nested inside the VLA pipeline: it shares the backbone's parameter layout as its output space, is trained against targets derived from the backbone's task vectors, and is queried jointly with the backbone at inference. The framework operates in three stages (Fig.~ fig:method ): Skill Acquisition ( sec:method_acquisition ): fine-tune on each , then compress the resulting task vector into a sparse skill via drop-and-rescale. Skill Consolidation ( sec:method_consolidation ): train one nested hypernetwork to absorb all action-expert targets into shared parameters with task embeddings. Skill Generation ( sec:method_generation ): at inference, query with the target task identity to generate the action-expert delta, retrieve the compressed VLM delta, and compose both updates with the frozen base. Skill Acquisition sec:method_acquisition The acquisition stage produces, for each task, a sparse skill representation that the hypernetwork can later be trained against. It comprises two steps: independent fine-tuning to obtain , and drop-and-rescale compression to turn into the compact . Independent fine-tuning. For each , we fine-tune to obtain and the task vector . We make no assumption on the training signal: may be obtained via supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or any combination thereof, as long as all are derived from the same . This decoupling matches the data-silo realities of robotics, where specialized skills are often trained independently in their native pipelines. Drop-and-rescale compression. A naive option is to use the dense as the hypernetwork target, but this is prohibitive in both memory and learnability for VLA backbones with billions of parameters. We observe that VLA fine-tuning deltas exhibit a sparse-magnitude-dominated structure: a small fraction of elements concentrate the bulk of the delta's energy, while the rest behave like low-amplitude noise; in contrast, LLM SFT deltas are typically denser and benefit from quantization-plus-low-rank schemes such as D-QRELO~ li2026d . We compared low-bit quantization, low-rank decomposition, and drop-and-rescale on VLA deltas and found drop-and-rescale dominates the fidelity-versus-compression trade-off ( app:compression ); we adopt it throughout

title: CoEvolve: Self-Evolving Code Policies from Skills to Strategies for Humanoid Robots
summary: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action Models (WAMs) have expanded the manipulation and whole body capabilities of individual robots. Yet a single robot remains limited by its embodiment, and many real world tasks require capabilities that can only emerge through cooperation. Existing multi robot frameworks largely emphasize task decomposition, allocation, and replanning, while providing limited support for adapting executable coordination when physical execution deviates from the intended behavior. We present CoEvolve, a framework that represents team coordination as executable code over fixed robot motor skills. CoEvolve introduces Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, where a multimodal foundation model instantiates coordination strategies through motion primitives, semantic objectives, temporary robot roles, and bounded execution parameters. Physical verification evaluates each executed transition, rejected behaviors trigger structured coordination revision from an accepted checkpoint, and verified experience is retained to guide subsequent decisions. We evaluate CoEvolve with two simulated Unitree G1 humanoids transporting a freely supported rigid payload through constrained corridors. Across 15 base task runs with three multimodal backbone families, CoEvolve completes 8 tasks, with every backbone achieving end to end success. Additional evaluations yield verified placement on two additional corridor layouts and after both same-backbone and cross-backbone experience initialization, while exposing persistent limitations in motion precision and contact stability. These results support executable coordination as a practical interface for adapting long horizon multi robot collaboration under shared physical constraints.

Introduction sec:introduction Recent advances in robot foundation models have equipped individual robots with increasingly general visuomotor capabilities, enabling them to follow language instructions and perform diverse manipulation tasks~ brohan2022rt,brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0 . Yet some physical tasks require capabilities that cannot be provided by one robot alone. Transporting an extended object through a constrained environment, for example, requires coordinated support, relative motion, corner negotiation, and placement~ de2023centralized,pandit2025multibiped . Collaboration is therefore not simply the aggregation of individual skills. Robots that can independently walk, turn, and move laterally must still determine how to combine these capabilities while carrying a shared object. We view this formation of team behavior as a form of co-becoming: effective cooperation is realized through the changing relationship between individual capabilities and the shared physical state. This motivates our central question: given fixed individual motor skills, how can an agent instantiate and revise executable team coordination as a shared physical task unfolds? Multi-robot planning methods address task decomposition, allocation, and collaboration through structured and language-model planning ~ cai2025mrbtp,mandi2024roco,kannan2024smart, liu2025coherent,yuan2025remac , while learned coordination methods optimize joint or decentralized policies through training~ zhang2026halo,doshi2026chorus . In parallel, agents improve textual skills, memory systems, and executable implementations through feedback and experience sharing~ yang2026skillopt,zhang2025memevolve,weng2026gea . Code as Policies and subsequent robot programming systems also generate and revise executable behaviors through interaction~ liang2023code,fu2026capx,lu2026aspire,xiao2026enpire . We study a complementary challenge: revising coordination when robots are physically coupled through a shared payload. In this setting, an individual action can alter both a teammate's support conditions and the feasibility of subsequent joint motion. As a result, a valid task plan does not guarantee that the current coordination pattern remains executable. The key challenge is therefore to instantiate joint behavior from fixed motor skills and revise the relevant coordination relation when physical execution deviates, for example when unequal displacement disrupts formation or a constrained turn requires temporary support and mover roles. We introduce , a framework for adapting executable team coordination during shared physical tasks. The evaluated setting provides simulator measurements and route references, while the model determines how these capabilities should be combined within the resulting physical constraints. Our Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution mechanism uses physical execution evidence to determine which aspects of coordination should change. A rejected transition triggers a revision to the maneuver, the relationship between robot roles, or the execution parameters. Revised policies are evaluated after restoration of the latest accepted simulator checkpoint. Verified outcomes also contribute complementary forms of experience: abstract coordination records guide subsequent decisions, while accepted executable examples inform code generation. Foundation model and motor policy weights remain fixed. The adaptation concerns the task plan, instantiated coordination strategies, and stored experience rather than the acquisition of new motor skills. title: SkyAgent: Revisable Target Memory for Continuous Aerial Search
summary: Continuous aerial search builds target hypotheses from sparse, viewpoint-dependent observations. When later evidence contradicts a stored hypothesis, however, the candidate can remain available to the planner and continue triggering approach or verification actions. We call this trajectory-level failure false candidate persistence (FCP). We equip SkyAgent with Revisable Target Memory (RTM), which associates evidence with persistent candidates, discounts correlated views, and revises each candidate through Tentative, Confirmed, and Rejected states. The key interface binds every generated waypoint to its source candidate: rejection therefore invalidates stale goals, while conservative reactivation protects temporarily occluded targets. Across four splits from the CityAVOS, UAV-ON, and OpenUAV benchmarks, our SkyAgent equipped with RTM outperforms all competitors, improving SR by 2.90--6.31 points while substantially reducing Behavior-FCP and post-contradiction travel with a low false-rejection rate. Across 35 matched real-world DJI scenarios per method, RTM consistently improves task success and behavioral reliability, further validating its state-to-action correction under physical deployment conditions.

Introduction sec:intro In a representative aerial search, a distant rectangular region is logged as a target candidate. A later side-angle view reveals that the region is a facade reflection, not the target. This revision problem is central to continuous aerial object search: the physical target is static, but evidence about each candidate shifts as the vehicle approaches, changes viewpoint, or encounters occlusion ji2025cityavos,xiao2025uavon,wang2024openuav . The agent rarely sees decisive evidence in a single frame; a distant shape, a brief gap in foliage, or an intermittent specular return may be all that a long trajectory provides. Existing aerial agents have made progress on two fronts. Memory-based methods retain observations across frames through asynchronous maps, octree representations, or filtered write-in~ zhang2026apex,zhou2026octmem,ji2025cityavos . Verification-based methods seek additional viewpoints before committing to a stop or reconsider a selected snapshot before executing it~ jang2026contextnav,cao2025cognav,ren2024explore, wang2026scope . Both fronts focus on the forward direction: building or validating confidence before a decision is made. We focus on what happens after: when a later view contradicts a candidate already sitting in persistent memory, can the system actually change that memory and cancel the goals it generated? In the systems we study, the answer is often no---the candidate remains available to planning even after a closer view proves it wrong. We define false candidate persistence (FCP) as a trajectory-level failure: after a candidate receives sufficient reference contradiction, it stays in the active plan (State-FCP) or again induces approach, revisit, or confirmation actions (Behavior-FCP). FCP is not a transient detector error, which is a wrong observation in a single frame; it is a known-wrong hypothesis that continues to consume distance, time, and planning cycles through stale memory state. Figure~ fig:problem illustrates this failure and its correction. The fix is not more storage. It is different memory semantics: candidates should be revisable hypotheses, not committed facts. A candidate must retain both supporting and opposing evidence, discount redundant adjacent frames, and expose an explicit lifecycle state to the planner. Changing a score alone is not enough; when a candidate is rejected, every pending waypoint it sourced must be invalidated before the next planning cycle. At the same time, rejection must not be permanent, because temporary occlusion and low-quality frames can produce misleading negative evidence. We equip the execution backbone with Revisable Target Memory (RTM). Candidate Evidence Memory associates observations with persistent candidates, groups them by independent viewpoint, and accumulates signed evidence. Revise-and-Suppress maps accumulated evidence to lifecycle states through a state-dependent transition function and cancels all stale waypoints on rejection. The existing fast search policy, event trigger, inspection skills, and safety-projected controller remain as execution infrastructure; candidate truth state is managed exclusively through RTM. Our contributions are three: (1)~we identify false candidate persistence (FCP) as a trajectory-level failure distinct from transient detection errors, and introduce complementary state-, behavior-, and cost-level measures that separate a stored false hypothesis from one that still affects flight; (2)~we propose Revisable Target Memory (RTM), which couples candidate lifecycle revision to planner binding: rejecting a candidate invalidates every unexecuted goal it sourced, while conservative reactivation permits recovery after new independent positive evidence; (3)~we evaluate RTM through natural FCP prevalence, controlled comparisons and mechanism ablations on three aerial benchmarks, and 35 matched DJI scenarios per method (Table~ tab:main ). title: From Sliding Windows to Self-evolving Lifelong Memory: A Dual-perspective Survey of Memory Paradigms for Long-Horizon Robotics VLA Models
summary: Long-horizon robotic tasks expose a fundamental limitation of current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models because their restricted temporal context pre-vents effective accumulation and reuse of past experiences. As a result, memory has become a fundamental component for enabling embodied agents to perform long-horizon reasoning and adaptive decision-making. This survey presents a systematic taxonomy of VLA memory mechanisms based on memory scope and persistence, categorizing existing approaches into five representative paradigms and one emerging frontier. Based on this taxonomy, we compare representative VLA memory systems in terms of memory characteristics, architectural com-plexity, and open-source maturity, revealing a clear trade-off in which increasing architectural complexity is generally accompanied by decreasing open-source ma-turity. Finally, we discuss the key challenges in building full-lifecycle memory systems, including efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolu-tion. Overall, this survey provides a unified perspective on memory architectures for VLA agents and offers insights into the development of lifelong embodied in-telligence.

title: LAW: Unifying Language, Action, and World Modeling for Agentic Physical Intelligence
summary: World-action models jointly predict actions and future world states, but long-horizon manipulation further requires language reasoning to plan subtask objectives, assess execution progress, and guide action selection. We present LAW, a closed-loop VLM--WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. Within the LAW agent, a hybrid-expert vision-language model plans the remaining subtasks, estimates the values of and fuses actions proposed by a world-action model, and asynchronously assesses execution status to support continued execution and subtask transitions. Within the world-action model, Mixture-of-Transformer Experts integrates modality-specific and shared computation for joint video--action modeling. Dual-stream hierarchical visual memory maintains temporal context for both models, while subtask-local value learning aligns action evaluation with semantic objectives and preserves supervision from successful prefixes of failed trajectories. LAW achieves 94.21% average success across 50 RoboTwin tasks. Replacing the WAM backbone with OpenWAM-$alpha$ further raises the average success rate to 95.56%, establishing a new open-source state of the art on RoboTwin. Despite having only 2B parameters, our VLM also outperforms variants using Embodied-R1.5 and GPT-5.5 High. On three long-horizon real-robot tasks, LAW achieves 65% average success, compared with 28.33% for $pi_{0.5}$ and 25% for Fast-WAM.

After reaching for an object, a robot must decide whether the grasp actually succeeded; after a successful grasp, it must recognize that the task has entered a new stage; before executing the next motion, it must choose among several physically plausible actions according to the current objective~ ahn2022saycan,huang2022innermonologue . Errors in any of these decisions compound over time. Consequently, local action quality alone does not determine task success. A capable agent must maintain a persistent account of task progress, connect that account to action generation, and revise its decisions when execution departs from expectation~ liu2023reflect,torne2026mem . Vision-language-action policies connect semantic representations to control~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pizero , while world-action models learn action-conditioned scene evolution and executable behavior~ zhu2025uwm,zheng2025flare,zhang2026lingbotva,yuan2026fastwam . These models substantially improve action generation, but long-horizon deployment exposes a complementary systems problem: reasoning and control must remain aligned as the task evolves. A language plan generated once at the beginning cannot determine whether its intermediate steps were completed~ huang2022innermonologue , and an action generator conditioned only on the current observation may not know which visual changes matter to the larger goal~ shi2026memoryvla . Placing a planner before a policy therefore leaves three interfaces underspecified: how execution progress updates the plan, how candidate actions are judged against the current semantic objective, and how relevant history is retained without overwhelming either model. Our premise is that semantic subtask progress should serve as the temporal interface between language reasoning and world-action modeling. Subtasks provide more than a decomposition of the instruction: they define when the agent should advance its plan, which outcomes a candidate action should optimize, and which observations should remain salient in memory. This view reveals that computations occur at different rates. State assessment should run continuously without blocking control, candidate evaluation should occur whenever the WAM proposes a new action chunk, and planning should operate at the semantic task scale rather than at every control step. The challenge is coordinating reasoning and control, rather than invoking a larger reasoner at every step. We instantiate this principle in LAW, a closed-loop VLM--WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress, as summarized in Fig.~ fig:law-teaser . The LAW agent uses a hybrid-expert VLM with role-selected planner, state, and value experts on a shared frozen backbone. The planner predicts the remaining semantic subtasks; conditioned on the current subtask, the WAM generates diverse action chunks; the value expert ranks and fuses them; and execution status is assessed asynchronously to determine subtask completion. Once the current subtask is completed, the planner predicts the next subtask and the agent switches to it; otherwise, the agent continues executing the current subtask. The LAW agent coordinates planning, action selection, and execution monitoring at different frequencies, using feedback to continue or switch subtasks. To strengthen joint world and action modeling, we introduce Mixture-of-Transformer Experts (MoTE) into the WAM, yielding MoTE-WAM. MoT projects video and action features into a common attention space to exchange cross-modal information, but their subsequent transformations remain modality-specific. MoTE introduces shared experts to further transform these cross-modal representations, alongside video-private and action-private experts that preserve modality-specific computation. The shared experts learn common temporal and physical structure across predicted scene dynamics and robot actions, strengthening video--action joint modeling beyond information exchange through attention alone. Long-horizon execution also requires memory aligned with subtask transitions. Separate hierarchical memory streams for the VLM and WAM retain recent observations and full-resolution states at subtask boundaries, while compressing older history to preserve relevant context across subtasks. To better exploit failed trajectories when training the value expert, we introduce subtask-local value learning, which terminates returns at semantic boundaries. This preserves positive supervision from successfully completed subtasks within failed episodes, rather than assigning zero value to all their actions. We evaluate LAW on 50 RoboTwin~ chen2025robotwin tasks, the RoboDojo~ chen2026robodojo capability benchmark, and three long-horizon real-robot tasks containing up to nine semantic subtasks. LAW achieves 94.21 average success on RoboTwin, 2.38 percentage points above Fast-WAM, without robot-data pretraining. Replacing the WAM backbone with OpenWAM- further raises the average success rate to 95.56 , establishing a new open-source state of the art on RoboTwin. Despite having only 2B parameters, our VLM outperforms variants using Embodied-R1.5 and GPT-5.5 High within the same LAW framework. On RoboDojo, LAW achieves leading performance across capability dimensions among methods without additional robot-domain or embodied-interaction pretraining. On the three long-horizon real-robot tasks, LAW achieves 65 average success, compared with 28.33 for and 25 for Fast-WAM. We also conduct extensive ablation studies to validate the effectiveness of each component. Our contributions are: We introduce LAW, a closed-loop VLM--WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. The LAW agent coordinates planning, asynchronous completion assessment, and value-guided action fusion for long-horizon execution. We introduce MoTE, dual-stream hierarchical memory, and subtask-local value learning to support progress-aware control: MoTE strengthens joint video--action modeling through shared and modality-specific experts; dual-stream hierarchical memory preserves task-relevant history and subtask-boundary observations; and subtask-local value learning retains positive supervision from completed stages of failed trajectories. We demonstrate LAW's effectiveness on RoboTwin, RoboDojo, and long-horizon real-world manipulation through extensive experiments and ablation studies. Integrating OpenWAM- achieves 95.56 average success on RoboTwin, establishing a new open-source state of the art and demonstrating LAW's extensibility to stronger pretrained WAMs. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models for Robot Control Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) provide semantic representations that vision-language-action (VLA) policies connect to executable control~ driess2023palme,zitkovich2023rt2,li2024roboflamingo,kim2024openvla,black2024pizero , supported by heterogeneous robot datasets and generalist pretraining~ openx2023rtx,octo2024 . RT-2 and OpenVLA represent actions as tokens, whereas couples a VLM with a flow-matching expert for continuous action generation~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pizero . Beyond action parameterization, CoT-VLA predicts intermediate visual subgoals~ zhao2025cotvla , while VEGA aligns visual-encoder outputs with geometry-aware features before vision-language fusion~ wang2026vega . These approaches strengthen semantic transfer and spatial grounding, motivating complementary mechanisms for coordinating instructions, execution progress, and action selection over extended tasks. Language-guided systems connect reasoning to execution through affordance-based skill selection, environmental feedback, action hierarchies, and spatial value maps~ ahn2022saycan,huang2022innermonologue,belkhale2024rth,huang2023voxposer . SayCan grounds language plans in learned affordances, whereas VoxPoser translates language-specified objectives and constraints into spatial maps for trajectory optimization~ ahn2022saycan,huang2023voxposer . In navigation, NavCoT structures decisions through future imagination and observation matching~ lin2025navcot , while Memoir retrieves environmental and behavioral experience using imagined states~ xu2026memoir . Although navigation differs from continuous manipulation, these studies illustrate how intermediate reasoning and selective memory access support sequential decisions. For long-horizon robot policies, the corresponding challenge is to retain task-relevant history and execution feedback when semantic stages extend beyond individual action chunks~ shi2026memoryvla,torne2026mem . title: Frame-Consistent Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting from Sparse Unposed Images
summary: Feed-forward Gaussian models have made novel view synthesis almost instantaneous. Feed-forward methods predict Gaussians directly, either in two stages or in a single merged pass. Using two separately trained models is attractive because each can specialize in its own objective: one for accurate pose estimation and the other for high-quality reconstruction, rather than forcing a single jointly trained network to compromise between the two. A natural instantiation pairs a frozen pose estimator, VGGT, with a frozen reconstruction backbone, TokenGS. Prior work, such as VGGT-X and 3R-GS, also adopts a two-stage design, but attributes the resulting quality degradation to noisy pose estimates and introduces learned refinement. We show that this is not the primary source of the problem. Through per-camera analysis across 107 scenes from two datasets, DL3DV and MipNeRF360, using COLMAP poses as the reference, we find that the rotation error after alignment is small (median 1.6 degrees), whereas the translation scale is offset by a large, dataset-consistent factor. Controlled ablations over 140 DL3DV scenes show that the primary obstacles are two integration failures rather than pose error: a coordinate-frame inconsistency and a translation-scale mismatch, both of which can be corrected deterministically. With these fixes, a frozen VGGT driving a frozen TokenGS achieves 22.47 PSNR, within 0.51 dB of the COLMAP reference, with no additional training, when poses are estimated from all scene views. In the sparse setting, where reconstruction uses only four context images under the standard pose-free protocol, the same pipeline matches this all-view quality, yielding a fully COLMAP-free pipeline without any refinement step.

Using two separately trained models is attractive because each can specialize in its own objective: one for accurate pose estimation and the other for high-quality reconstruction, rather than forcing a single jointly trained network to compromise between the two. Controlled ablations over 140 DL3DV scenes show that the primary obstacles are two integration failures rather than pose error: a coordinate-frame inconsistency and a translation-scale mismatch, both of which can be corrected deterministically. With these fixes, a frozen VGGT driving a frozen TokenGS achieves PSNR, within ~dB of the COLMAP reference, with no additional training, when poses are estimated from all scene views. In the sparse setting, where reconstruction uses only four context images under the standard pose-free protocol, the same pipeline matches this all-view quality, yielding a fully COLMAP-free pipeline without any refinement step. Introduction sec:introduction With 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs , recent advances aim to make explicit reconstruction faster and more reliable without degrading quality. Feed-forward Gaussian methods~ noposplat,tokensplat,kang2025selfsplat,pf3plat,uni3r use feed-forward networks, MLPs and transformers to predict Gaussians directly, with small or no refinement iterations, which makes reconstruction faster. Conventional 3DGS~ 3dgs instead does reconstruction in two stages: during the first stage, COLMAP~ colmap estimates the poses, during the second stage it initializes the Gaussians and refines them with iterative optimization. Recent feed-forward methods fall into two families by how the pose and reconstruction components are trained. One family trains a single network end-to-end: NoPoSplat~ noposplat , AnySplat~ anysplat , TokenSplat~ tokensplat , SelfSplat~ kang2025selfsplat , PF3plat~ pf3plat , and Uni3R~ uni3r jointly learn geometry and Gaussian prediction, so that pose estimation and reconstruction are optimized together within one model. The other family composes separately-trained models: VGGT-X~ vggt_x and 3R-GS~ 3rgs take poses from a pretrained geometry estimator and add a distinct learned refinement or optimization stage on top. Our work belongs to the latter family structurally, but connects two frozen pretrained models through deterministic operations alone, with no refinement or training. Given images and poses, TokenGS~ tokengs unlike other feed-forward GS methods, predicts a fixed number of Gaussians, without other models that change the number of Gaussians based on image content. Its transformer architecture uses poses as Plücker ray embeddings to fuse with the image patches. But it requires already estimated poses, which is a blocker for using the model as a direct feed-forward pipeline that predicts Gaussians from unposed images. An easy integration is to use a direct pose estimator such as VGGT~ VGGT , MASt3R~ MASt3R , or DUSt3R~ DUSt3R to predict the pose. In this way we can use two separately trained large models, each for its specific objective: one for pose accuracy, one for good reconstruction. However, directly integrating the estimated context view poses degrades reconstruction quality substantially~ vggt_x, 3rgs , which raises concerns about the pose quality of these pose estimators. Prior work largely addresses the degradation from imperfect geometric initialization through learned or optimization-based refinement. VGGT-X~ vggt_x keeps the VGGT~ VGGT predictions fixed and applies adaptive global alignment using XFeat correspondences, jointly refining the camera parameters with an epipolar loss, followed by MCMC-based 3DGS training with joint pose optimization. 3R-GS~ 3rgs initializes from MASt3R-SfM~ MASt3R-SfM poses and addresses their imperfect initialization through MCMC-based pose optimization, an MLP-based global pose refiner, and a rendering-free epipolar geometric constraint. VGGS~ vggs , in contrast, leverages VGGT's multi-view geometric priors for sparse-view surface reconstruction, using an anchor-calibrated depth estimation scheme and a relative-depth consistency loss to align VGGT's depth predictions to the underlying surface. While it also contends with misalignment in VGGT's outputs, its focus is depth-level surface fidelity rather than the coordinate-frame and scale mismatch we identify when composing VGGT poses with a reconstruction backbone. Instead, we investigate the actual source of this mismatch, rather than fixing it implicitly with a refinement network. Through controlled analysis, we find that the failure is not caused by pose inaccuracy. After alignment, VGGT's rotation error is small, while its translations are offset from the backbone's expected distribution by a large, systematic scale factor. Our controlled ablation over 140 DL3DV scenes shows that the major obstacles to merging VGGT and TokenGS are not pose errors, but two integration failures: coordinate-frame inconsistency and translation-scale mismatch, both of which admit deterministic fixes. With frame consistency and scale correction, we compose two frozen pretrained models (VGGT and TokenGS) with no retraining or fine-tuning. When VGGT estimates poses from all scene views, the composition reaches within 0.51 dB of the COLMAP-initialized baseline. The same fixes hold in the sparse setting, where VGGT estimates poses from only the context views, maintaining quality with no per-scene optimization. In summary, our contributions are: We diagnose two integration failures in two-stage feed-forward 3DGS systems: coordinate frame inconsistency and translation scale mismatch, and show via controlled ablation that these, not pose error, cause the quality collapse when connecting frozen feed-forward pose and reconstruction models. We provide a per-camera error decomposition across 107 scenes (DL3DV~ dl3dv , MipNeRF360~ mipnerf360 ): rotation error is small (median ), while translation scale is offset by a large, dataset-consistent factor (approximately ). We introduce deterministic, training-free fixes, frame consistency and scale correction, reaching PSNR on 140 DL3DV~ dl3dv scenes, within ~dB of the COLMAP~ colmap reference, with poses estimated from all scene views, while maintaining the same inference speed. We show the fixes hold in the sparse setting: whereas the result above estimates poses from all scene views, here VGGT processes only the 4 context views together with one target at a time (the standard pose-free protocol), yet reconstruction quality is maintained, giving a fully COLMAP-free pipeline. Related Work sec:relatedwork Radiance Field Representation Radiance field reconstruction has developed along two main lines: implicit representations such as NeRF~ nerf , and explicit ones such as 3DGS~ 3dgs . Both typically rely on COLMAP~ colmap to initialize camera poses. Given the posed images, an implicit network is trained to represent the scene, or explicit primitives learn features that represent it, in both cases optimized independently for each scene. Because this per scene optimization is slow, reconstructing a scene takes considerable time, which is prohibitive for real time applications. Subsequent work reduces this cost through faster optimization and compact representations~ scaffoldgs, lightgaussian, minisplatting , but the dependence on COLMAP~ colmap poses and per scene optimization remains. With the advancement of transformers, several methods predict pose and reconstruction in a single forward pass. We review these methods in the following subsections. Feed-Forward Pose and Geometry Estimation As networks become more powerful, 3D pose estimation can be solved directly by a neural network, almost entirely removing the time-consuming post-processing. DUSt3R~ DUSt3R , MASt3R~ MASt3R , and VGGT~ VGGT have shown results comparable to SfM based methods~ colmap, sfm, vggsfm . However, DUSt3R~ DUSt3R and MASt3R~ MASt3R process only two images at a time and rely on post-processing to reconstruct larger sets, fusing pairwise reconstructions into a global one. VGGT~ VGGT instead processes one, a few, or even hundreds of views jointly in a single forward pass, achieving higher pose accuracy and often outperforming optimization-based alternatives without further processing. We build on VGGT as a state-of-the-art feed-forward pose estimator; independent evaluations~ wu2025evaluation report its reliability in sparse-view settings. VGGT~ VGGT expresses all cameras in the coordinate frame of the first input view and is trained with scale-normalized supervision: two properties central to the integration failures we analyze in Section~ sec:method . Feed-Forward Gaussian Reconstruction A growing body of work builds Gaussian reconstruction on top of feed-forward geometry models~ VGGT, MASt3R, DUSt3R . These methods fall into two groups by how they use poses. Unified feed-forward networks. One group trains a single network end-to-end to output Gaussians directly from unposed images. AnySplat~ anysplat adopts a VGGT-inspired geometry transformer and retrains it to jointly predict Gaussians and camera poses, while TokenSplat~ tokensplat trains a unified architecture with learnable camera tokens and an asymmetric decoder for joint pose and Gaussian estimation. SelfSplat~ kang2025selfsplat learns pose and Gaussian prediction jointly in a self-supervised manner, using a matching-aware pose network and depth refinement to couple geometry and reconstruction without ground-truth poses. Pose estimator with per-scene optimization or refinement. A second group takes geometry or poses from a feed-forward estimator and then applies classical iterative optimization or learned refinement. VGGT-X~ vggt_x augments VGGT with adaptive global alignment (via XFeat correspondences and an epipolar objective) and robust MCMC-3DGS training for dense-view synthesis, and 3R-GS~ 3rgs adds an MLP-based global pose refiner and a rendering-free epipolar constraint to MASt3R-SfM initializations. Both attribute the difficulty to imperfect or noisy pose estimates: VGGT-X frames VGGT's outputs as degrading initialization-sensitive training and reports that a gap to COLMAP persists even after adaptive alignment. VGGS~ vggs instead uses VGGT's geometric priors for a different task, sparse-view surface reconstruction, calibrating depth against multi-view anchors with a relative-depth consistency loss; its concern is depth-level surface fidelity rather than the coordinate-frame and scale mismatch we identify. Common to these methods is the assumption that feed-forward geometry cannot be used as is: unified networks resolve this by retraining, while the second group relies on per scene optimization or learned refinement on top of a separate estimator. Whether two independently pretrained feed-forward models: a pose estimator and a reconstruction backbone, can be connected directly and kept frozen has not been studied. We show that they can. The obstacles are coordinate frame inconsistency and translation scale mismatch, and once these are addressed deterministically, frozen VGGT poses drive a frozen TokenGS to within 0.51~dB of the COLMAP reference with no training, and the same fixes hold in the sparse setting

title: Beyond Success Rate: Interventional Evaluation of Memory in Vision-Language-Action Systems
summary: When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role? Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide offsetting gains and losses. We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) for vision-language-action (VLA) systems to address four questions: (1) Does memory provide a net benefit? (2) Under what conditions does memory help? (3) Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? (4) Are these effects specific to task-relevant facts? At the retrieval interface, we compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect over fact-preserving replacements. To examine when memory helps, we introduce ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in current observations. The full memory configuration raises task success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under shared recorded executions. These results show that correct history can support robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.

Introduction sec:intro A robot's current observation may omit information needed to act: an earlier visual cue, a previous episode's experience, or a fact retained across tasks. Vision--language--action (VLA) systems therefore augment policies with memory banks, event keyframes, or temporal representations memoryvla,kemo,hamlet , experience retrieval memer , and external text records harnessvla . These mechanisms aim to turn history into useful evidence for current decisions. Their value is often evaluated through memory ablations and task success memoryvla,kemo . Such gains show improved performance, but do they establish use of task-relevant stored facts (Figure~ fig:teaser a)? Three distinctions prevent that inference. First, enabling memory can change both information and computation. Second, an unchanged success rate can hide gains on some trials and losses on others predictionchurn . Third, changing memory can alter behavior even when a replacement preserves the target fact or introduces only a small numerical perturbation. History can also support shortcuts, as shown by causal confusion and copycat behavior in imitation learning causalconfusion,copycat . Behavioral sensitivity alone does not establish use of task-relevant facts. Conversely, an undetected net gain does not imply that memory has no effect. Interpretation also depends on whether current observations already reveal the answer, whether an intervention reaches the reader, and whether stored facts remain valid. title: Look Before You Act: Bridging Active Perception and Vision-Language-Action Models via Observation-Aligned Data Adaptation
summary: Robots manipulating objects in clutter must decide not only how to act, but also where to look. Although active camera motion can expose an occluded target, it may move the robot into an initial observation-state distribution that differs from the manipulation policy's training distribution. We identify this problem as first-frame distribution sensitivity: under perturbed starts in LIBERO, naively prepending camera repositioning to pi_0.5 reduces success from 46.3% to 11.5%. We introduce ActiveAlign, a data-adaptation framework that trains a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy from the states at which active perception terminates. A learned viewpoint module first generates a camera trajectory. Offline, ActiveAlign uses closed-loop alignment to connect the trajectory endpoint to an existing demonstration, replays the remaining manipulation trajectory, and retains successful continuations for fine-tuning. At deployment, the same viewpoint module precedes the adapted VLA without modifying its architecture. Across 40 LIBERO tasks, ActiveAlign achieves 70.7% success with pi_0 and 72.7% with pi_0.5, outperforming their standard-training baselines by 40.0% and 26.4% respectively. Matched-state and data-matched controls support gains beyond prefix shortening and generic viewpoint augmentation; OpenVLA and GR00T N1 also show the same trend. Success rate under physical occlusion in real world increases from 35/90 to 83/90. These results show that active perception benefits manipulation when policy training is aligned with the observation and robot-state distribution induced by viewpoint selection.

INTRODUCTION Effective manipulation begins with an observation that supports the intended action~ liu2025reasongrounder,liu2025neural . A robot asked to retrieve fruit from a container or grasp a cup behind clutter may need to move its camera before it can see a useful approach direction. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ black2024pi0,kim2024openvla,intelligence2025pi05,team2024octo,liu2025trivla provide a powerful interface from visual observations and language to robot actions, but their input is still determined by where the robot looks. Repositioning an existing wrist camera is an appealing way to expose the target before manipulation. The resulting system must therefore solve two connected problems: selecting an informative view and continuing the task from the state produced by that selection. The most direct composition is to let an active-perception (AP) module improve the view, then hand control to a VLA trained on conventional demonstrations. Our experiments reveal a counterintuitive outcome: this composition can substantially reduce task success. Under a shared perturbed-start LIBERO protocol, falls from 46.3 to 11.5 average success after camera repositioning, and falls from 30.7 to 7.0 . The qualitative examples in illustrate the tension: a policy can act from a familiar but occluded view, yet struggle to exploit a view selected to reveal the target. Improving the observation and making it usable by the action policy are distinct requirements. We study this interface through first-frame distribution sensitivity. Here, the first frame is the observation at the handoff from active perception to manipulation. Wrist-camera motion changes image location, scale, and occlusion together with arm configuration and the relationship to the remaining task. A policy must consequently infer a suitable continuation from a different combination of visual and proprioceptive cues. Action chunking~ zhao2023aloha,chi2023diffusion can propagate an early error through the actions executed before the next observation, even when later decisions use fresh images. This motivates examining the joint observation--action interface; a difference between first-frame image distributions alone does not establish the cause of every failure. Our experiments therefore pair the failure observation with controls that separate viewpoint information from robot-state progress and data volume. The central design insight is that the deployment viewpoint policy is available during data construction. Rather than requiring a manipulation learner to accommodate arbitrary sensing motions, we can expose it to successful continuations from the endpoints of the very module it will encounter at inference. This turns the composition problem into a question about supervision: how can existing demonstrations be made to begin where active perception stops? Demonstration-generation methods such as MimicGen and DemoGen~ mandlekar2023mimicgen,xue2025demogen motivate reusing recorded behavior, while the present setting adds a specific constraint: the starting observation and state are chosen by a task-conditioned camera policy. Visual augmentation alone does not supply the actions needed to continue from that state. ActiveAlign constructs these continuations offline. Given scene RGBD and a language instruction, a learned module predicts a wrist-camera trajectory. In a restored environment, we execute the trajectory and match its endpoint to a nearby end-effector state in an early demonstration prefix. Closed-loop alignment bridges the residual gap, after which the recorded manipulation suffix is replayed. Successful alignment-and-replay trajectories become training data for the VLA. The active approach replaces part of the original demonstration, while the recorded continuation teaches the policy how to proceed after that approach. At deployment, the same viewpoint module runs once before object contact; the adapted VLA then manipulates using fresh observations. The procedure changes training data and policy weights while preserving the VLA architecture. Replay feasibility is essential to this construction. End-effector proximity does not ensure that object and contact states agree, so nearest-state matching alone cannot validate a continuation. Successful replay filters the candidate endpoints and limits the training distribution to states for which usable supervision can be reconstructed. ActiveAlign consequently applies to resettable simulators and reconstructable physical workcells. This requirement belongs to offline data collection: deployment requires neither scene reset nor expert replay. The resulting scope is pre-manipulation view selection, with longer-horizon tasks testing the lasting value of that initial view rather than continuous response to moving occluders. Our evaluation follows this reasoning from composition failure to controlled explanation and physical validation. On LIBERO Spatial, a matched-state camera-extrinsics control holds the demonstration step and manipulation suffix fixed and reaches 54.6 , compared with 78.2 for ActiveAlign. Data-matched random views and broad viewpoint jitter reach 58.0 and 61.4 , respectively. These comparisons support a benefit from the informative, deployment-matched observations beyond shorter demonstrations and generic coverage. Across four suites, ActiveAlign improves and by 40.0 and 26.4 percentage points; OpenVLA and GR00T N1 extend the evidence to different action formulations. Initial-occlusion simulation tasks, diverse physical tasks, and endpoint perturbations further characterize when the construction is useful and where it breaks down. Our contributions are threefold: We characterize the failure of naive composition of active perception and VLAs, and test competing explanations through matched-state and data-matched controls. We introduce observation-aligned demonstration adaptation, connecting active-view endpoints to successful manipulation through prefix matching, closed-loop alignment, and replay filtering. We evaluate the construction across four VLA backbones, 40 LIBERO tasks, initial occlusion, and physical manipulation, with sensitivity studies that quantify the feasibility--diversity trade-off and endpoint error tolerance. title: AWAM: Active Trajectory-Conditioned View Imagination for Robust Robot Manipulation
summary: Rapid progress in embodied intelligence has enabled increasingly capable robots to follow language instructions and manipulate diverse objects. However, strong results in structured environments do not automatically transfer to open-world conditions, where clutter, occlusion, and changing viewpoints can obscure the spatial relationships required for action. To address this perceptual gap, a virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced. AWAM, an Active World-Action Model actively plans where to observe and imagines what will be seen along the planned trajectory before acting. Task-related virtual camera motion is predicted and used as a structured query into a geometry-conditioned world model, producing a reusable spatial prior for manipulation, which is later compressed into a fixed memory and fused with live observations through cross-attention for diffusion-based action prediction. AWAM achieves competitive success rates with 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials. These results support improved robustness to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts, addressing part of the gap between structured manipulation and less controlled environments.
