Introduction Embodied intelligence has advanced rapidly through large-scale robot learning, vision--language pretraining, and generative action modeling. Increasingly capable policies can translate language goals and visual observations into manipulation behaviors across diverse tasks~ rt1,rt2,octo,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,chi2023diffusion . However, much of this progress is evaluated in relatively structured settings in which camera configurations, scene layouts, and task-relevant objects remain sufficiently observable. Occlusion-focused and distribution-shift benchmarks expose a complementary limitation: once deployment becomes less structured, an unfavorable camera pose, clutter, or a shifted layout can hide the target or interaction region and remove the evidence required for control~ li2026liberoocc,fei2026liberoplus,bai2026tvve,liu2025reasongrounder,liu2025neural . This creates a perceptual bottleneck rather than only an action-modeling bottleneck. More expressive action models alone cannot directly recover scene evidence that is absent or highly ambiguous in the input, so performance gains obtained under well-observed scenes may not transfer to open-world conditions with incomplete visibility. Several lines of work have begun to address this problem. Physical active perception acquires additional evidence by moving the camera or robot, but introduces extra execution steps and can alter the robot or scene state. Virtual-view methods avoid this cost by selecting or synthesizing complementary observations. Candidate-view approaches choose from predefined cameras~ liu2026activevla,xu2026univiewvla ; TVVE predicts task-conditioned virtual poses and re-renders reconstructed geometry~ bai2026tvve ; and world-action models such as Motus and Fast-WAM exploit predictive visual modeling to strengthen action representations~ motus,fastwam . These directions establish the value of additional visual context, yet the underlying limitation is not fully resolved: virtual perception is often restricted to isolated views, reconstruction-based rendering cannot reveal surfaces absent from the initial geometry, and predictive world models are commonly organized around action-induced futures rather than deliberate viewpoint queries. To address these questions, task-conditioned virtual active perception is formulated as trajectory-conditioned view imagination. Instead of selecting a single view or a small set of independent poses, a virtual camera trajectory specifies how perception should evolve to expose task-relevant evidence. Such a trajectory can reorient toward a target, approach fine interaction geometry, or move around an occluder when no single viewpoint is sufficient. Importantly, the predicted trajectory is never physically executed; it serves only as a sequence of virtual queries, thus retrieving the available evidence and learned spatial priors into a representation that better supports control, separating perceptual exploration from robot motion. Based on this formulation, is introduced as an Active World-Action Model that realizes the virtual-perception process before closed-loop control. A task-conditioned trajectory predictor first produces virtual camera poses for better observation from the initial RGB-D image and language instruction. The calibrated observations are then back-projected into coarse 3D geometry and rendered along the predicted path. A geometry-conditioned world model fills unsupported regions and produces multi-view latent features, which are compressed into a persistent world memory. During manipulation, live static- and wrist-camera observations retrieve relevant predictive context from this memory, and a diffusion policy generates short-horizon action chunks in closed loop. The resulting design uses world modeling as an internal perceptual mechanism for asking where to look and what would be seen, rather than as a prediction of the robot's executed future. Evaluation is conducted across three simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation. Success reaches 75.9 on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4 on LIBERO-Plus, on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4 in real-robot trials. On LIBERO-Occ, removing the entire predictive-memory branch reduces average success by 11.5 percentage points, and replacing learned task-conditioned virtual trajectory with sampled viewpoints reduces it by 5.7 points. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of learned virtual camera motion and persistent predictive memory for manipulation under incomplete visibility. The contributions are threefold: A trajectory-conditioned virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced for manipulation, replacing isolated or physically executed viewpoint acquisition with a continuous sequence of task-directed virtual queries. is proposed to transform the predicted observation trajectory into geometry-consistent multi-view representations and compress them into persistent world memory as a reusable spatial prior for manipulation under partial observability. Extensive evaluations across three challenging simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation demonstrate strong performance under occlusion and distribution shifts and confirm the benefits of learned camera motion and predictive memory through ablations. Related Work sec:related_work Robot learning and action generation. Large-scale robot policies map visual observations and language instructions directly to actions. Recent VLA models and diffusion-based policies improve generalization, action representation, and efficient decoding through large-scale pretraining and expressive generative objectives~ rt1,rt2,octo,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,chi2023diffusion,fast,openvla_oft,liu2025trivla,liu2025spatial . These methods primarily focus on how actions are represented and learned from available observations. In contrast, targets the perceptual evidence supplied to the policy, constructing additional task-conditioned spatial context when relevant scene information is poorly observed or occluded. Multiview manipulation under occlusion. Occlusion can be mitigated by acquiring or synthesizing complementary visual evidence through multiview perception, viewpoint selection, and imagined views~ liu2026activevla,bai2026tvve,li2026liberoocc,xu2026univiewvla . Existing approaches typically rely on additional sensing, reconstructed views, or a small fixed number of generated observations. instead predicts a task-conditioned virtual camera trajectory and consolidates the generated multi-view sequence into persistent world memory for closed-loop manipulation. This formulation turns occlusion handling into trajectory-conditioned predictive perception, where the model jointly reasons about where to observe, what would be observed, and how this information should support subsequent control. World models for robotic manipulation. Recent video diffusion and world models have shown strong capability in modeling long-horizon visual dynamics, while text-, action-, and camera-conditioned variants further enable controllable prediction of future or novel observations~ zhang2025gendop,zhang2026worldstereo,liu2026omnicam . Predictive world models provide representations of how visual observations may evolve and have increasingly been integrated with robot control. Video Prediction Policy~ hu2025vpp conditions control on features learned from predictive video modeling. Motus~ motus unifies visual understanding, video generation, inverse dynamics, and action prediction within a latent world-action model. Fast-WAM~ fastwam separates the benefits of video co-training from explicit test-time future generation and shows that strong action prediction can be retained without iterative future-video rollout. Unlike approaches centered on predicting the future scene induced by robot actions, uses world modeling as a form of active perception. A task-conditioned camera trajectory specifies where the current scene should be queried, and a geometry-conditioned world model predicts visual representations along this trajectory. These representations are consolidated into a compact world memory and reused throughout manipulation rather than interpreted as the robot's executed future. Rather than relying on the initial viewpoint alone, a task-conditioned camera trajectory is predicted to specify where additional virtual observations should be queried for better scene perception. Demonstrated wrist-camera paths provide proxy supervision for task-relevant virtual queries. title: HexaShell: A Thin Harness for Exploring the Limits of VLM Agents as Robot Coding Agents
summary: Agents built on vision language models (VLMs) now compete with learned policies on robot manipulation leaderboards. We ask how far a coding agent can go when it controls a robot instead of a computer, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin: it only turns the agent's commands into robot motion. The agent drives a robot with two arms through one command line. It sees three RGB cameras and knows their calibration. After each failed attempt, the agent reads the log, finds the cause, and writes or fixes small programs called tools. Agents built on vision language models have now started to compete. On RoboDojo robodojo2025 , the model we use reaches 22.5 without tools of its own, choosing gripper targets through a fixed harness written by the benchmark's authors zhang2026unexpected . Coding agents suggest another route. In a software repository, a coding agent reads the code, runs it, reads the error and fixes the code, and the fix stays. Recent work has begun to let coding agents write and revise robot tools and programs urai2026,gao2026selfevolving,liu2026rapid,kang2026encore . We ask how far a coding agent can go when it works on a robot in the same way, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin. The agent gets one command, robo, three RGB images with their calibration, and a manual of one page. The harness turns commands into joint motion and does nothing else. After a failure, an optimizer agent of the same model reads the episode as it would read a failing test, writes or fixes a tool with its unit tests, and the layout is tried again ( ). Both agents are Codex with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort. The hard part is turning pixels into positions. In a repository, everything the agent works on is text it can read exactly. On a robot, the agent sees objects as pixels, but every command needs a position in the world, to about a centimetre for a grasp. Vision language models are known to judge such distances poorly chen2024spatialvlm,cheng2024spatialrgpt . The standard observation has no depth. Our tools use triangulation instead. The cameras are calibrated, and the robot knows where its wrists are. A point that two cameras see lies where their rays meet, and a point on a measured plane, such as the table, lies where its ray meets that plane hartley2004multiple . When one view is not enough, the robot moves a wrist camera to get another. This is active perception bajcsy1988active , and on a benchmark it has a price: the motion uses action steps, and every task has a step limit. We build the tools on ten layouts of each task, freeze them, and test them on ten new layouts. A thin harness and a short repair loop for robot coding agents. The harness gives an unchanged coding agent one command line to the robot and makes no decisions for it. All that the agent learns is kept as small tools with unit tests, which the next episode loads. After a failure, a second agent of the same model edits one tool and the same layout runs again. The model picks a pixel on the target, and the tool turns it into a position. title: X-Splat: Unified Gaussian Splatting for Joint RGB and X-ray 3D Reconstruction

summary: Jointly reconstructing RGB and X-ray provides new insights by connecting external appearance with internal structure, enabling a more complete understanding of real-world objects than single modality. Yet existing methods train separate models per modality and suffer from redundant geometry, alignment artifacts, and loose coupling that limits cross-modal insight discovery. We propose a unified representation in which all Gaussian primitives share a single set of geometric parameters, with only surface-proximal primitives additionally carrying appearance attributes. We perform cross-modal registration through clean multi-view stereo and X-ray geometric proxies instead of aligning two sets of optimized Gaussians, improving alignment stability. We then jointly optimize the unified representation via supervision from both modalities, complemented by a surface-depth consistency loss derived from X-ray geometry to guide RGB reconstruction. Experiments on the InsideOut dataset and our Flower & Insect dataset show that our framework achieves more robust cross-modal alignment, higher RGB rendering quality without compromising X-ray reconstruction, and a more compact representation than maintaining two independent geometries.

Each Ours/InsideOut panel shows three vertical strips at the same viewpoint: pure RGB / overlay / pure X-ray. fig:teaser Introduction Real-world objects are both surface and interior: we readily see a flower's outer petals, but not the structure within. Yet existing 3D reconstruction typically captures only one of the two at a time. RGB cameras record the external appearance through surface reflection, while X-ray imaging penetrates objects to reveal their internal volumetric structure through attenuation, leaving the two as separate digital records of the same physical object. We pursue a unified 3D representation that natively captures both, enabling consistent rendering of an object's exterior and interior from any viewpoint (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Such a unified representation supports applications such as digital cultural heritage~ bossema2024enabling , industrial inspection~ bergmann2019mvtec , and physically-grounded visualization~ ni2024phyrecon , providing a more complete understanding of real objects than either modality alone. Existing 3D reconstruction work has developed each modality along a separate track. RGB-based approaches built on neural radiance fields (NeRF)~ mildenhall2021nerf and Gaussian splatting~ kerbl20233d reconstruct external surfaces but treat the object interior as unobserved space. X-ray-based methods such as NAF~ zha2022naf , X-Gaussian~ cai2024radiative , and R -Gaussian~ zha2024r recover internal density distributions but provide no surface appearance. Training separate models per modality is a natural starting point, yet such a decoupled approach keeps two independent representations of the same object with no cross-modal alignment, increasing parameter count and preventing consistent rendering of external appearance and internal structure. A more principled direction is to design a single framework targeting RGB and X-ray jointly, and the recent InsideOut~ lee2025insideout is the first such attempt. It trains a separate Gaussian set per modality and bridges them through hierarchical alignment between the two optimized representations. While this design takes a first step toward joint reconstruction, it leaves several aspects underexplored. First, the two Gaussian sets independently model the same underlying geometry, doubling the parameter footprint. Second, the alignment operates on optimized Gaussian primitives that are the outcome of geometric and appearance fitting rather than a faithful description of the object's surface, and contain floaters and optimization artifacts, leading to surface-to-interior misalignment that compromises applications requiring aligned internal-external display, such as digital cultural heritage~ bossema2024enabling . Finally, although the scene geometry is accurately recovered from X-ray, it is still underutilized in RGB optimization, leaving RGB weakly supervised and limiting surface fidelity in applications such as industrial inspection~ bergmann2019mvtec . To address these limitations, we present , a unified Gaussian framework for joint RGB-X-ray 3D reconstruction. Our design is based on a simple observation: although RGB images arise from surface reflection and X-ray images from volumetric attenuation, both are ultimately conditioned on the geometry of the same physical object. This shared geometric origin suggests that the cleanest design is not to model each modality with its own independent geometry, but to let the two modalities share a single geometric representation while specializing only the attributes that genuinely differ between them. Concretely, we propose a unified Gaussian representation in which all primitives share a single set of geometric parameters, and only primitives close to the surface carry appearance attributes, reflecting the physical fact that RGB observations arise primarily from surface reflection. This eliminates the redundancy of maintaining two independent geometries and lets gradients from both modalities flow into the same shared geometry. To bring the two modalities into a common coordinate frame, we register them through clean geometric proxies derived directly from the input data, namely a multi-view stereo (MVS)~ yao2018mvsnet, gu2020cascade, yang2020cost, peng2022rethinking, cao2022mvsformer point cloud from the RGB views and a mesh extracted from the X-ray reconstruction, rather than aligning the already-optimized Gaussians. Finally, we exploit the shared geometry to enable joint optimization across both modalities, complemented by a surface-depth consistency loss using X-ray-derived surface geometry to supervise RGB rendering. In summary, our contributions are: A unified Gaussian representation with shared geometric parameters and surface-restricted appearance attributes, enabling compact joint modeling of external appearance and internal volumetric structure. A geometry-based alignment pipeline using clean MVS and X-ray proxies to register two modalities, avoiding the surface-to-interior misalignment that arises when registering two sets of already-optimized Gaussians. A joint optimization scheme where both modalities update shared parameters via their respective objectives, complemented by an X-ray-derived surface-depth consistency loss. We evaluate on the InsideOut dataset~ lee2025insideout and a new Flower Insect dataset combining existing flower scans~ ijiri2014flower with newly captured insect specimens, broadening evaluation to natural objects. Our method achieves more robust cross-modal alignment, better RGB rendering quality without compromising X-ray reconstruction, and is more compact than two independent models. A parallel line replaces the volumetric formulation with neural implicit surfaces~ wang2021neus,yariv2021volume to recover sharper geometry. More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl20233d represents the scene with explicit Gaussian primitives and a tile-based rasterizer, achieving real-time rendering at comparable visual quality, with Mip-Splatting~ yu2024mip addressing aliasing under varying sampling rates. Subsequent work has improved surface fidelity by reformulating the primitives as 2D disks~ huang20242d or regularizing them toward the underlying surface~ guedon2024sugar . Internal Structure Reconstruction subsec:internal-recon X-ray and computed tomography (CT) reconstruction~ gordon1970algebraic, li2023sparse, yu2025x2 recovers the internal density distribution of an object from projection measurements. Classical analytical methods such as FDK~ feldkamp1984practical remain the standard for cone-beam CT, producing volumetric reconstructions in closed form when projections are dense. To handle sparse-view settings, NAF~ zha2022naf adapts a neural attenuation field to fit projection measurements with a continuous network representation, and SAX-NeRF~ cai2024structure employs a line-segment Transformer to capture spatial structure from X-ray projections. title: Enhancing Visual Task-Redirection Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models via Closed-Loop Optimization
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable language-guided robot manipulation, but remain vulnerable to visual attacks that undermine user control over robot behavior. Prior studies optimize visual perturbations using fixed target supervision. However, the perturbation can change earlier actions and, in turn, the physical states reached later. As the attacked trajectory evolves, this supervision may no longer match the behavior needed at the states actually reached. Accurately matching these targets can therefore fail to advance the attacker-specified task. Even with suitable supervision, reducing average matching error does not ensure sustained task progress. The robot may still fail at a critical stage, and further updates can disrupt previously successful behavior. To address these limitations, we propose TRACO, a framework that enhances existing targeted visual attacks through closed-loop optimization. Its Execution-Driven Supervision rebuilds supervision for the states reached under attack to guide subsequent updates. Within this framework, Progress-Guided Selection focuses updates where progress stalls while maintaining supervision on the earlier behavior needed to reach that point. Experiments across VLA models and simulation environments show improved task-redirection success with TRACO, highlighting the security implications of closed-loop attack optimization.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse manipulation tasks from natural-language instructions~ openvla,pi02024 . During execution, they repeatedly use new camera observations to decide how to continue the task. This visual feedback allows the robot to adapt its actions as the scene changes~ rt2 . However, visual perturbations can change the actions the model generates~ tma,lu2026uparfas . By changing the robot's actions, an attack can also change the physical states and observations encountered later. These altered observations then guide the robot's subsequent actions. The attack can therefore influence how the robot proceeds through the task and what it ultimately accomplishes. Understanding these closed-loop effects is important for assessing the security of VLA systems. Recent studies have demonstrated the vulnerability of VLA models to visual attacks. Many of these attacks aim to make the user's intended task fail~ xu2025edpa,lu2026uparfas,fu2026vlahijack,wang2026poap . Some pursue this goal by inducing prescribed actions or trajectories~ tma,tex3d . These targets specify how the robot should deviate, but not what task it should complete instead. In contrast, TRAP studies task-level behavior hijacking, where success requires the robot to complete an attacker-specified task~ trap . Its supervision includes reasoning and action targets. In both cases, target supervision is fixed before optimization. It comes from prescribed action targets or pre-collected target rollouts. This raises a central question: can fixed supervision still guide the robot to complete the target task as the attacked trajectory evolves? sec:motivation The challenge is that optimizing the perturbation can change the very states on which the robot must act. When attacks use pre-collected target rollouts, perturbation updates rely on the recorded observations and target outputs. During execution, however, the updated perturbation can lead the robot to states different from those in the recorded rollouts, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:closed-loop-motivation (a). To continue the target task from these attack-induced states, the robot may need to behave differently from what the recorded targets specify~ laskey2017dart . Better matching to these fixed targets therefore need not translate into successful closed-loop execution~ zhang2026actionchunking,bansal2019chauffeurnet . Figure~ fig:closed-loop-motivation (b,c) illustrates this gap for action matching on recorded observations in one scene. This motivates using execution feedback to refresh target supervision as the attacked trajectory evolves. Execution feedback must also guide where optimization should focus and what earlier behavior it should preserve. Even with suitable targets, matching some behaviors more accurately can lower the average loss while an unresolved error still blocks task progress~ bastani2018viper,park2025sqil . For example, in a pick-and-place task, better matching of placing actions cannot compensate for a failed grasp: the robot must grasp the object before it can place it. Because the same perturbation affects all execution steps, an update intended to improve the blocked behavior can also weaken earlier successful behavior. Optimization should therefore focus near where progress stalls while retaining the earlier behavior needed to reach that point. To address these problems, we propose TRACO (Task-Redirection Attacks via Closed-loop Optimization), a framework that enhances existing visual attacks through execution feedback. Its Execution-Driven Supervision (EDS) rebuilds target supervision for the states reached under the current perturbation. These targets guide subsequent perturbation updates. The resulting execution, in turn, supplies the states for rebuilding target supervision, closing the loop between attack optimization and execution. Within this loop, Progress-Guided Selection (PGS) selects states for supervision to advance the target task while retaining earlier behavior. Using a successful target rollout as an ordered reference, PGS identifies the matched prefix and progress frontier of the attacked rollout. Supervision at the frontier focuses updates on the behavior needed for further progress. Meanwhile, continued target supervision along the prefix helps retain the earlier behavior needed to reach the frontier. TRACO thus constructs and organizes supervision from actual execution. Existing targeted attacks can use this supervision with their own alignment objectives. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose TRACO, a framework that extends visual task-redirection attacks on VLA models to closed-loop optimization. Its Execution-Driven Supervision (EDS) replaces fixed targets with supervision reconstructed at the states reached under attack. Existing attacks can thus account for the state changes they induce while retaining their alignment objectives. We introduce Progress-Guided Selection (PGS) to organize supervision according to ordered trajectory progress. It combines frontier supervision with prefix supervision along the current attacked rollout. This design helps advance the target task while retaining earlier behavior under a visual perturbation shared across execution steps. We evaluate TRACO across diverse VLA models and simulation environments. Results from simulation and real-robot experiments demonstrate TRACO's effectiveness for visual task redirection, highlighting the value of closing the loop between attack optimization and execution. Related Work sec:related-work Vision-Language-Action Models Generalist robot policies learn language-conditioned manipulation from diverse robot data~ brohan2023rt1,openx2024,ghosh2024octo . VLA models such as RT-2 and OpenVLA build on pretrained vision-language representations and predict actions autoregressively as discrete tokens~ rt2,openvla . In parallel, diffusion-based action generation has been adopted in both visuomotor policies and VLA models~ chi2023diffusionpolicy,wen2025tinyvla,li2024cogact,wen2025diffusionvla . title: TransNav: Transformer-Based End-to-End Navigation Method for Static and Dynamic Quadrotor Obstacle Avoidance
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Published in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Obstacle avoidance for autonomous quadrotors in cluttered environments remains challenging, especially when both dense static obstacles and moving obstacles are present. Existing methods are often tailored to either static or dynamic settings, which always limit their adaptability across diverse environments. This paper presents TransNav, a transformer-based end-to-end navigation method for quadrotor obstacle avoidance in both static and dynamic environments. TransNav employs a patch-based point-cloud encoding scheme that combines local feature extraction with global contextual modeling, enabling compact yet informative environment representation. The method integrates perception and navigation in a single architecture and directly predicts a finite-horizon action sequence, from which the first action is executed. Moreover, we develop an unsupervised learning strategy by incorporating a lightweight point-mass dynamics model, which directly optimizes trajectory-level costs over the predicted sequence through numerical gradient propagation. Thus, the policy can be efficiently trained without expert demonstrations. Simulation and real-world experiments show that the proposed method achieves strong performance in dense static environments and competitive obstacle-avoidance capability in dynamic scenarios, while maintaining low inference cost for onboard deployment.

Introduction utonomous drones are widely deployed in scenarios such as exploration 2021FUEL , search and rescue alsamhi2022uav , and inspection xu2023vision . These environments are filled with densely distributed small obstacles and randomly moving dynamic obstacles, which require drones to perceive their surroundings in real time and generate immediate control commands to navigate safely. Traditional methods typically rely on manually designed perception-decision-control pipelines, where computational delays and cumulative errors severely degrade performance. In contrast, learning-based end-to-end navigation methods directly map raw sensory input to control commands, enabling high-performance real-time flight yu2024mavrl, song2023learning, lu2024you, hu2025seeing, zhang2026high, xu2025flying, xu2025flow, fan2025flying . Recent studies using depth images lu2024you , optical flow hu2025seeing , or 3D LiDAR point clouds xu2025flying as perception data have demonstrated outstanding results in dense environments. Achieving a good balance between static-scene navigation and dynamic-obstacle avoidance remains difficult. Approaches designed for static environments lu2024you , xu2025flying react insufficiently to rapidly moving obstacles, while a few methods xu2025flow tailored for dynamic scenarios tend to overfit to motion features, leading to degraded performance in dense static environments. Moreover, training strategies of the navigation policies in xu2025flow , fan2025flying rely heavily on training settings dominated by dynamic obstacles, which increase computational burden and fail to cover the full diversity of real-world obstacle motions, resulting in limited generalization. These limitations make it difficult to deploy an end-to-end policy reliably across a wide range of realistic conditions. To address these limitations, we propose TransNav, a transformer-based end-to-end navigation method for quadrotors using LiDAR point clouds. TransNav is designed to provide a more general policy for obstacle avoidance across both settings. On the one hand, to overcome the insufficient response speed of existing static-scene methods to moving obstacles, TransNav predicts a finite-horizon action sequence at a high frequency, achieving more effective reactions to obstacle motion. On the other hand, to ensure navigation performance in dense static environments, TransNav employs a patch-based LiDAR representation that preserves local geometric details while allowing global spatial context to be modeled compactly. Specifically, raw point clouds are first converted into a high-resolution distance map and then partitioned into patches inspired by vision transformers. A lightweight CNN and self-attention mechanism are further used to jointly encode local obstacle structure and longer-range spatial dependencies. In addition, an efficient unsupervised training strategy is introduced to directly optimize trajectory-level costs over a finite prediction horizon. By integrating a lightweight point-mass dynamics model into the learning pipeline, gradients of the full action sequence can be backpropagated directly without expert demonstrations or critic networks. This design enables fast convergence while maintaining strong sim-to-real generalization. The quadrotor used in real-world environments is shown in Fig. fig:uav . The main contributions are summarized as follows: A transformer-based end-to-end navigation architecture is proposed for quadrotors, which fuses patch-based LiDAR distance-map representations with sampled reference-trajectory states to predict a finite-horizon action sequence within a unified framework. A lightweight perception-to-action pipeline is developed, which predicts action sequences for high-frequency receding-horizon execution. It improves the response ability of the policy to moving obstacles while maintaining strong navigation performance in dense static environments. An efficient unsupervised training strategy for the proposed action-sequence policy is developed, which incorporates a lightweight point-mass dynamics model to directly optimize trajectory-level costs over the predicted action sequence without expert action labels. Related work Static Environment Navigation In static cluttered environments, most methods rely on optimization-based navigation pipelines that decompose the problem into perception, planning, and control. For example, Zhou et al. zhou2020ego integrate grid maps with an optimization-based planning algorithm to enable real-time trajectory generation using onboard sensors such as LiDAR or depth cameras. However, high-resolution grid maps increase computational burden, while low-resolution maps fail to effectively preserve perception of fine-grained obstacles. In recent years, an increasing number of approaches ren2025safety , wang2022geometrically use flight corridors to characterize free space, improving the efficiency of interaction between motion planning algorithms and environmental perception. Nevertheless, flight corridors implicitly filter environmental topological information, leading to loss of solution space. Recent work has increasingly explored learning-based navigation methods for static environments. Zhang et al. zhang2025corb use safe flight corridors as environmental representations, generating smooth B-spline trajectories through learning-based control point optimization. This approach achieves robust navigation in static cluttered environments and can avoid some low-speed objects. However, this approach is constrained by the speed of corridor generation, preventing rapid responses to high-speed obstacles. More recently, end-to-end approaches based on depth images lu2024you and LiDAR point clouds xu2025flying directly map perception inputs to control-related outputs, showing faster response times. However, due to the lack of high-frequency planning capability or temporal prediction ability, neither of the works is suitable for highly dynamic environments. In comparison, our method achieves reactive avoidance of moving obstacles by predicting a future action sequence at a high frequency. Dynamic Environment Navigation To address the need for obstacle avoidance in dynamic obstacle environments, researchers develop some dynamic obstacle detection algorithms to perceive and predict moving obstacles for safe trajectory planning. Lu et al. lu2024fapp employ a clustering algorithm to segment dynamic obstacles from point clouds and utilize a Kalman filter to estimate the velocity of moving objects. Subsequently, an optimization algorithm is applied to generate the drone's trajectory. However, the point cloud-based dynamic perception methods are computationally intensive, and the accuracy significantly decreases when dynamic objects move at high speeds. Furthermore, solving model predictive control and polynomial optimization problems is highly time-consuming for complex scenarios. Unlike approaches relying on active perception, Liu et al. liu2023integrated propose an integrated planning-and-control architecture. By combining high-frequency control responses with trajectory prediction capabilities, it enhances the system's reaction speed to dynamic obstacles, enabling avoidance of suddenly appearing moving objects. Recently, significant progress has been made in learning-based dynamic obstacle avoidance. Xu et al. xu2025navrl propose the NavRL framework, which estimates the states of dynamic obstacles and integrates a velocity-based safety shield to maintain safe flight in dynamic environments. However, due to limitations in object perception algorithms, real-time performance degrades significantly as the number of dynamic obstacles increases, making it challenging to maintain safety in highly dynamic settings. To enhance response ability, an increasing number of end-to-end approaches have been applied for obstacle avoidance in dynamic environments. Fan et al. fan2025flying achieve dynamic obstacle perception by compressing multiple frames of previously scanned point clouds into a 2D obstacle map, then directly mapping the perceived information and state information into acceleration commands to control the quadrotor. Xu et al. xu2025flow encode LiDAR point clouds into low-resolution, fixed-shape distance maps, combining them with multi-frame point stream information extracted by pre-trained NeuFlowV2 to form a perceptual representation of environmental changes. title: Learning Robot Metareasoning: Adaptive Computation Budgets for Real-Time Control
summary: Planning while moving faces an historical trade-off between deliberation and reactivity. A planner running concurrently with execution needs time to compute, so the robot must commit to an open-loop action chunk for that duration: a longer commitment buys a better plan at the cost of feedback frequency. Existing controllers fix this action commitment, and consequently the computation budget, before deployment. However, the optimal computation time is highly state-dependent (due to factors such as unmodeled dynamics, safety constraints, and marginal optimisation gains), i.e. dynamic, therefore offline static tuning risks leaving systems blind during critical maneuvers or unable to find global effective solutions. We cast the identification of the optimal computation budget as a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) in which a single decision defines both the robot action commitments and the time allocated to the solver. To solve this, we train a reinforcement-learning policy conditioned on the current state, the executing plan, and inexpensive planner statistics. Across ground-robot navigation, agile quadrotor flight, and contact-rich manipulation, the learned policy changes its budget with the demands of the scenario, discovering efficient reasoning patterns that outperform fixed-budget baselines. https://lorenzomagnino.github.io/learning-robot-metareasoning-review/

Biological agents dynamically arbitrate their cognitive resources, continuously balancing rapid, reactive responses against slower, deliberate reasoning based on environmental uncertainty and temporal constraints~ otto2019opportunity, daw2005uncertainty . This adaptive allocation represents a fundamental speed-optimality trade-off where extended deliberation is penalized by elapsed time~ keramati2011speed, shenhav2017toil . The value of computation (VOC) formally characterizes this trade-off between the marginal gain in decision optimality and the cost of deliberation~ russell1991metareasoning,hay2012selecting . Traditional metareasoning frameworks assume a frozen world state during planning, requiring an explicitly defined cost function to penalize extended computation, a paradigm we refer to as the economic value of computation. Embodied autonomous agents, conversely, operate in continuous time where this assumption fails. Because the robot and its environment evolve concurrently with the planner's execution, heuristic timing penalties are unnecessary. Instead, the physical dynamics inherently penalize computational delay through unmitigated state drift, thereby hindering high-frequency reactivity and reducing safety margins. We introduce this dynamic trade-off as the physical value of computation, formalized in Sec.~ subsec:smdp . As standard for computational efficiency, robots typically plan in receding-horizon: the system optimizes a trajectory over a finite horizon, executes the initial segment, and subsequently replans from the evolved state. Model predictive control (MPC) williams2017mppi,bharadhwaj2020cem commits to a single control step, resolving the problem at every control period, providing high-rate feedback around a nominal trajectory. Alternatively, action-chunking architectures generate a sequence of actions to execute in open-loop while the next plan is produced. This commitment can improve motion smoothness and sample efficiency zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion,black2024pi0 , yet fundamentally limits the system's ability to react to high-frequency disturbances or environmental changes. In both paradigms, the solver's computational budget and execution horizon are statically defined prior to deployment. Consequently, the robot lacks a principled mechanism to dynamically arbitrate when a state warrants extended deliberation for trajectory optimality versus when it necessitates rapid, reactive feedback (Fig. fig:hero ). Identifying an optimal static computation budget cannot be resolved via offline tuning. It is fundamentally a state-dependent quantity, dictated by the unmodelled dynamics, the proximity to state-space constraints, and the marginal optimality gained through additional solver iterations. Moreover, the budget choice cannot be assessed from the current state alone: its consequences propagate to future states throughout the episode, where they may influence later decisions and outcomes. We address these challenges by formulating adaptive computation budgets for real-time control as a semi-MDP over decision epochs. At each epoch, one decision sets both the open-loop execution horizon and the parallel computational resources allocated to solver. We then learn this decision from experience with an RL policy (Fig.~ fig:overview ). Because a chunking policy emits several actions at once, a mechanism is required to cover the gap while the next chunk is generated. Unlike our approach, none of these methods couples the execution length with the solver's computation budget, so a larger commitment cannot be leveraged to compute a better plan. Event- and self-triggered MPC frameworks dynamically determine when to replan rather than solving at every control step, preserving feasibility and stability of the system sun2019robust . Alternative approaches dictate the replanning interval based strictly on safety, defining it as the maximum duration the current trajectory can be executed while a collision-free fallback remains available magdici2017horizon . However, these triggering mechanisms are designed fundamentally to conserve computation subject to a baseline guarantee, treating the underlying optimizer as an oracle whose solution quality does not improve with additional allocated time. Metareasoning prices computation by the improvement in the decision quality it produces, net of the cost of running it~ russell1991metareasoning,hay2012selecting . This principle underlines anytime algorithms, deliberation scheduling~ dean1988timedependent,zilberstein1996anytime , and learned computation budget~ callaway2018bmps . In these conventional formulations, the world is treated as frozen while the agent deliberates, so the cost of thinking is an explicit penalty chosen by the designer to trade against the expected benefit. title: EmbodiedMidtrain: Bridging the Gap between Vision-Language Models and Vision-Language-Action Models via Mid-training
summary: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) inherit their visual and linguistic capabilities from Vision-Language Models (VLMs), yet most VLAs are built from off-the-shelf VLMs that are not adapted to the embodied domain, limiting their downstream performance. In this work, we propose EmbodiedMidtrain to bridge the gap between VLMs and VLAs. We first characterize the data distribution gap between them, showing that VLA data occupy compact regions that are largely separated from the broader VLM distribution, while the degree of alignment varies substantially both across and within VLM data sources. Then, we build a mid-training data engine that leverages a lightweight learnable proximity estimator to select the most VLA-aligned candidates from a large VLM pool, and produce EmbodiedMidtrain-1M, a VLM dataset that we further use to mid-train the VLM before downstream VLA fine-tuning. Experiments on both simulated robot manipulation benchmarks and real-world tasks show consistent VLA performance gains over off-the-shelf checkpoints across VLM backbones and VLA action heads. These gains extend to downstream tasks not used to guide data selection. Further analysis reveals that mid-training provides a stronger initialization for VLA fine-tuning, with gains emerging from the earliest steps and widening throughout training. Moreover, the data engine captures both dataset-level and sample-level alignment signals, favoring spatial reasoning over text-centric tasks while preserving the diversity of the VLM data. We will release all code, data and models for future research.

Project page: Introduction sec:intro Recent advances in robotics foundation models have given rise to Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs), which unify vision perception, language understanding, and action generation within a single model to enable generalist robot control across diverse tasks, environments, and embodiments~ kim2024openvla, black2024pi0, gemini_robotics_2025 . Most VLAs leverage Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as their backbone, aiming to inherit rich visual and linguistic representations that facilitate rapid adaptation to embodied settings~ kim2025oft, pi05, gr00tn1_2025 . Despite this progress, a fundamental gap exists: most VLAs initialize from general-purpose off-the-shelf VLMs that are not tailored toward embodied action generation. VLM pretraining~ llava,pmlr-v202-li23q,Qwen-VL covers broad vision-language tasks such as captioning, visual question answering, and document understanding, whereas VLA training consists of robotic manipulation trajectories grounded in physical interaction. This distributional mismatch means that, even when a VLM backbone provides a strong initialization for language and visual understanding, its internal representations may not be well-suited for the embodied reasoning that effective action generation demands~ yang2025vlaser . Bridging this gap remains an open challenge: simply fine-tuning VLMs on curated embodied data does not reliably translate into better VLA performance~ zhang2026vlm4vla , indicating the need for more principled VLM adaptation to the VLA domain. In this work, we present EmbodiedMidtrain, a mid-training framework that aligns VLM data distribution with the VLA domain, enabling VLAs for robot manipulation to truly benefit from the abilities of their VLM backbones. We begin with a deep analysis of the VLM-VLA representation gap and identify a core issue~(Figure~ fig:overview a): the two domains exhibit a significant data distribution discrepancy. VLA data form compact clusters that are largely separated from the broad, diverse VLM distributions~ xing2025shortcut ; yet this gap is not uniform, as some VLM samples are inherently more aligned with the VLA domain than others. This reveals that the bulk of VLM data concentrates on capabilities distant from VLA data, leaving downstream VLA fine-tuning to bridge a wide representational gap from a misaligned starting point. Leveraging this understanding, we develop a mid-training data engine that reshapes the VLM training distribution toward the VLA domain before fine-tuning begins~(Figure~ fig:overview b) to bridge the gap. The key idea is that, rather than training on all available VLM data indiscriminately, we can focus on the subset that is most useful for robotics by aligning with the target VLA distribution, producing a stronger, more relevant initialization for downstream VLA learning. Concretely, we propose a lightweight proximity estimator: a learnable classifier on frozen VLM features that learns to distinguish VLA data from VLM data, and whose predicted scores serve as a continuous measure of each VLM sample's closeness to the VLA domain. Top-scoring samples are then assembled into a curated mid-training mixture, and the VLM is mid-trained on this distribution-aligned dataset to serve as a better initialization for VLA fine-tuning (Figure~ fig:overview c). This pipeline is lightweight, effective, and requires no architectural changes to the underlying VLM or VLA. Experiments on Calvin ABC-D~ mees2022calvin , SimplerEnv Bridge~ walke2023bridgedata , and Libero-10~ liu2023libero show that our mid-trained 1.1B model achieves a significant performance boost~(Figure~ fig:overview d). Beyond raw performance gain, our analysis reveals several insights into what makes mid-training effective. First, the same curated data transfers across architectures: applying the mixture selected with InternVL3.5-1B to Qwen3VL-2B yields consistent gains, suggesting that proximity-based selection captures transferable properties across VLMs. Second, the learned proximity estimator substantially outperforms hand-crafted alternatives like feature-space distance and perplexity-based metrics. Third, training dynamics analysis shows that the mid-trained model outperforms the baseline from the earliest fine-tuning checkpoints and the gap widens over time, indicating mid-training provides a fundamentally better VLM initialization for VLAs. Our main contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=*,nosep] A proximity-based mid-training pipeline and dataset to bridge the VLM-VLA gap. We propose EmbodiedMidtrain, a mid-training pipeline with a data engine that learns a proximity estimator to score VLM samples by their closeness to the VLA domain, and selects the top-ranked candidates to curate a distribution-aligned mid-training dataset EmbodiedMidtrain-1M. Consistent VLA performance gains across backbones, action heads, and target tasks. Extensive experiments on simulation benchmarks (Calvin ABC-D, SimplerEnv Bridge, and Libero-10) and real-world tasks demonstrate that VLMs mid-trained on our EmbodiedMidtrain-1M dataset yield consistent improvements over the original backbone. We further demonstrate its transferability across VLM backbones, VLA action heads and data selection target tasks. Insights on better VLM initialization for VLAs. We show that mid-training produces an initialization whose advantages emerge from the earliest fine-tuning steps and amplify over time. We further demonstrate that the learned proximity estimation outperforms hand-crafted alternatives by capturing fine-grained alignment with the VLA domain. Related work Models. VLAs extend foundation models like VLMs to generate robot actions, leveraging the broad visual and language understanding inherited from VLMs~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,gr00tn1_2025 . Existing designs differ in backbone choice and action generation mechanism. Token-based approaches such as OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla discretize robot actions into tokens for autoregressive generation; OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025oft further introduces parallel decoding with learnable action embeddings for efficient continuous action prediction. Flow-matching and diffusion-based approaches such as ~ black2024pi0 and ~ pi05 instead adopt a VLM backbone (PaliGemma~ beyer2024paligemma ) paired with a continuous action generation head. More recent models such as GR00T N1~ gr00tn1_2025 employ a VLM backbone (Eagle-2~ li2025eagle2 ) with a dedicated cross-attention action decoder. While these designs differ architecturally, a common thread is that the VLM backbone is taken off-the-shelf from general-purpose training without specific preparation for the embodied domain, which brings a gap that our work identifies and addresses. Mid-training. Many VLMs adopt multi-stage training pipelines, where the model is further trained on curated vision-language data after initial multimodal pretraining or alignment and before final instruction tuning~ Qwen-VL,Qwen2-VL,internvl25 . In this paper, we refer to this intermediate stage as VLM mid-training. Similar to mid-training in LLMs, its goal is to adapt a foundation model toward desired domains or capabilities prior to final post-training or task-specific fine-tuning~ wang2025octothinker,grattafiori2024llama3herdmodels,hu2024minicpmunveilingpotentialsmall,olmo20252olmo2furious . Our work studies this paradigm in the embodied setting, where mid-training is used to bridge the data distribution gap between general VLM pretraining data and VLA fine-tuning data. -oriented VLMs. A broad line of work aims to improve VLMs' embodied capabilities, through both embodied-oriented dataset construction~ du-etal-2024-embspatial,zhou2025roborefer,chen2025robo2vlmvisualquestionanswering,pmlr-v270-yuan25c-robopoint and model-level adaptation~ cai2025spatialbot,ji2025robobrain,internvlam1 . Alternatively, Vlaser~ yang2025vlaser converts in-domain robot trajectories into VQA pairs for VLM fine-tuning. title: StopWatch: Goal Grounding for Object-goal Navigation
summary: Pretrained VLMs bring rich world knowledge and semantic priors to object-goal navigation, and fine-tuning a VLM into a navigation policy has become a common recipe. Despite this progress, success rates remain low, and it is unclear which capability these fine-tuned policies lack. Our diagnosis identifies goal grounding as the dominant failure. These policies explore well, yet often fail to notice that the goal is already in view or to estimate how far away it is. To address this failure, we ground the goal explicitly. Explicit grounding substantially improves success and reaches state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks across three scene collections. We also correct annotation defects in these benchmarks, so that future methods are evaluated more faithfully. Our analysis on the clean benchmarks shows that, with ground-truth grounding, our policy nearly matches the expert that generated its demonstrations, leaving the headroom in perception rather than policy learning. Our work points to goal grounding as a missing piece of object-goal navigation and offers a simple and effective solution to the task.

Introduction sec:intro Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) bring web-scale visual and semantic knowledge to embodied navigation. In object-goal navigation, where an agent must find an instance of a named object category in a novel scene, fine-tuning them on expert demonstrations has become a common recipe~ zhang2024uni,xiang2025navr2,chu2026abot,zhang2026qwen,wang2026lightnav,zhang2026embodied . Progress has come from larger demonstration sets~ zhang2024uni,zhang2026embodied,zhang2026qwen,chu2026abot and better modeling of the observation history~ zhang2024navid,zhang2024uni,zhang2026qwen , yet these policies still generalize poorly to unseen goal categories. Further scaling brings diminishing returns~ zhang2024uni,wang2026lightnav , and some observe that perception and grounding, rather than the navigation policy, limit performance~ xue2026omninav,chu2026abot . What is missing is a diagnosis of which capability these policies lack. In this paper we give that diagnosis and build an object-goal navigation system around it. Our diagnosis indicates these policies fail at goal grounding: determining whether the goal is in view and how far it is. These policies learn search well from demonstrations. They actually reach the goal far more often than they succeed ( e). An end-to-end policy can come within 0.25\,m of the goal in 76 of episodes yet succeed in only 52 ( ). In contrast, given the ground-truth semantics in view and distance to the goal, the same policy can have a success rate of 89 . Stopping at the right place thus turns out to be harder than reaching it. The diagnosis suggests a direct remedy. We make goal grounding explicit, so that before each action the agent states which objects are in view and how far the goal is, much like chain-of-thought reasoning in language models and embodied agents~ wei2022chain,zawalski2024robotic,lin2025navcot . Unlike free-form reasoning traces, which are generated by large VLMs and prone to noise~ zawalski2024robotic,xiang2025navr2,wang2025auxthink,gao2025octonav , our goal grounding is derived from the semantic and geometric labels of the training scenes. Every demonstration frame comes with its own ground-truth goal grounding at no extra labeling cost. At test time, the grounding text must be predicted, so we build a pipeline of two models with this text as their interface. A perception model predicts the grounding from RGB observations, and a policy model reads it alongside the observations to choose the next action. The two are trained separately, the policy on ground-truth grounding and the perception model on the same annotations. Goal grounding could also be learned inside a single end-to-end model as an additional output, but such a model navigates worse in our experiments. The pipeline reaches state-of-the-art success on six object-goal navigation benchmarks, 8.8 points above the strongest baseline on HM3D-OVON val unseen with corrected annotations ( ). These results reduce a long-standing failure of object-goal navigation to a concrete perception problem. Our contributions are threefold: We identify goal grounding as a missing piece for object-goal navigation. Policies often reach the goal but fail to stop, which can be mostly fixed by correct grounding. Guided by this, we build a two-model pipeline that makes goal grounding explicit, reaching state-of-the-art results on all benchmarked object-goal navigation tasks. We guide future work from two perspectives. We remedy annotation defects in existing benchmarks, so future methods are evaluated more faithfully. On the clean benchmarks, we show that the policy is already strong and the remaining headroom lies in perception. Related Work Embodied navigation tasks. Navigation tasks differ in how they specify the goal. Early tasks give the goal as coordinates or an image~ anderson2018evaluation, liu2025citywalker, zhu2017target, krantz2023navigating, liu2026wanderland . These tasks are less complex and addressed by large-scale reinforcement learning~ wijmans2020ddppo . Object-goal navigation names an object category and asks the agent to find any instance of it~ batra2020objectnav, yokoyama2024hm3dovon . The agent must search the scene efficiently, remember where it has been over long horizons, and recognize the goal once it comes into view. In the open-vocabulary setting, test goals include categories never used as goals in training. Like most recent work, we study navigation in continuous environments~ zhang2024navid, zhang2024uni, cheng2024navila , and focus on open-vocabulary object-goal navigation. Modular navigation systems. Modular systems decompose navigation into perception and planning modules~ chaplot2020semexp, ramakrishnan2022poni . Each module can be inspected on its own, and such systems transfer to real homes far better than end-to-end policies~ gervet2023navigating . Open-vocabulary models~ radford2021clip, liu2024groundingdino made this line zero-shot. Detectors localize the goal, and image-text similarity or LLM commonsense scores the frontiers to explore~ gadre2023cow, zhou2023esc, yokoyama2024vlfm . LLMs also plan in language, parsing instructions into landmarks or reading captions of the observations~ shah2023lmnav, zhou2024navgpt . Similarly, we make perception explicit, but only for the two cues our diagnosis finds missing. Unlike their planners, which act only on this interface by fixed rules, our policy sees every frame and learns search and stopping from demonstrations. VLMs for navigation. Rather than composing modules, recent work fine-tunes a single pretrained VLM into the navigation policy, relying on its world knowledge for what these tasks demand. This is now the dominant approach~ zhang2024navid, cheng2024navila, zhang2024uni, xue2026omninav, chu2026abot, zhang2026qwen, wang2026lightnav, zhang2026embodied . These policies follow the vision-language-action (VLA) model paradigm~ brohan2023rt, kim2024openvla , where the model is trained end-to-end by behavior cloning on expert demonstrations. However, such training has been shown to harm the model's semantic priors and language understanding~ fang2025intention, driess2025knowledge, zhou2025chatvla . We follow this line of work, but supervise perception explicitly with structured text instead of relying on action labels alone. Intermediate reasoning. Writing out intermediate steps before the output improves both language models~ wei2022chain and VLA models~ zawalski2024robotic . In navigation, policies likewise generate reasoning text before acting, either at inference or as training-time supervision~ lin2025navcot, gao2025octonav, wang2025auxthink . The content of this text is chosen by design, typically plans, subtasks, or instruction progress written by a larger model, without evidence of what the policy lacks. Our grounding text instead holds only the two cues our diagnosis finds missing, the semantics in view and the distance to the goal, both read from the scene annotations of every training frame. The base model supplies general visual knowledge, and millions of expert demonstrations supply the policy. Yet success on novel goals stays low, and further scaling returns little. Counterintuitively, the agent explores an unfamiliar scene like an expert, nears the goal, and does not stop. The pretrained knowledge does not turn into the right decisions. This section locates the root cause, derives our system from it, and fixes the evaluation. Problem setup sec:setup We study object-goal navigation zhu2017target,batra2020objectnav . In the task, an agent is dropped into an unfamiliar environment. It must find an instance of a goal category and stop near one within a step budget. In the open-vocabulary form of the task yokoyama2024hm3dovon , the goal at test time may be unseen in training. The task couples open-ended semantics with embodied spatial search. A household robot faces this problem when asked to fetch a towel in a home it has never seen. Following the dominant approach zhang2024navid,cheng2024navila,zhang2024uni , we train the policy by behavior cloning (BC) on demonstrations from a frontier-exploration expert~ yamauchi1997frontier . We fine-tune a pretrained VLM to predict the expert's next action from the goal and the history of observations. Failure analysis of existing methods sec:failure Reaching without stopping. =-1 Success in object-goal navigation has two requirements. The agent must reach the goal, and it must STOP there. Fine-tuned VLM policies mostly meet the first requirement and miss the second, which has long been noted as a distinct difficulty~ wasserman2022lastmile,song2023terminate . On novel goal categories, an end-to-end policy comes within 0.25\,m of a goal in 76 of episodes, yet succeeds in only 52 ( ). Near the goal it walks past without stopping. Most failures come from the model not knowing that it has arrived. Why stopping fails. The two requirements pose very different problems for behavior cloning. The expert explores each scene in the same way until the goal comes into view, so the cloned search works just as well for a new category. Stopping, in contrast, requires recognizing the goal, and has much sparser supervision. A demonstration has a single STOP at its end, and only for training goal categories. From this one action per episode, the policy must learn goal grounding, namely whether the goal is in view and how far it is. Imitation alone does not make the policy use the VLM's pretrained knowledge, so it fails to stop for unseen goals. Grounding restores stopping. To test whether goal grounding is what the policy lacks, we give the same policy the ground-truth grounding text before each action. On the same episodes, success rises from 52 to 89 , and failures after reaching the goal fall from 24 to 5 ( , bottom). Wrong stops disappear entirely, and every remaining failure is a timeout.
